gloss.def: A community-controlled service that represents Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
An offence with no mens rea and no defence of mistake.
Using the court's process unfairly or improperly, for example trying an accused who cannot get a fair trial or was brought to court unlawfully.
A person who helps an offender escape after the crime, knowing it was committed (s 349).
A person who counsels, procures or pays for the crime but is not present.
The physical element of a crime: a voluntary act, an omission where there is a duty to act, or a state of affairs.
A temporary court set up for one conflict, such as the ICTY.
Allowed to be used in court. Evidence must be relevant and not excluded by a rule.
Evidence a court may consider; evidence that is contaminated, unreliable or improperly obtained may be excluded (Evidence Act 1995).
A trial run as a contest between two sides (prosecution and defence) before a neutral judge, who rules on the law and evidence but does not investigate.
Since 1 June 2022, a person does not consent to sex unless they say or do something to communicate consent.
The age below which a child cannot be guilty of an offence. In NSW it is 10.
A circumstance that makes the offence more serious and the sentence heavier (s 21A(2)): violence, a weapon, in company, a vulnerable victim, on bail or parole.
A statement of what happened that both sides accept. The judge sentences on these facts.
Asking a higher court to review a conviction or sentence. Some appeals are 'as of right'; the High Court hears appeals only with special leave.
Taking a person into custody to bring them before a court; lawful without a warrant only under LEPRA s 99.
The principle in DPP v Carr (2002) that police should not arrest where a court attendance notice would do; codified in s 99 (2014).
A document from a magistrate or registrar naming the person and the offence and authorising police to arrest them.
Make a judgement of value, quality, outcomes, results or size.
A further discount for helping police or prosecutors, for example by giving evidence against others.
Australia's financial intelligence agency and anti-money laundering regulator.
The act was involuntary, for example sleepwalking or concussion.
The temporary release of an accused person awaiting trial, with or without conditions.
Requirements that manage risk: reporting, curfew, surety, residence, no contact, electronic monitoring, rehabilitation (s 28).
The criminal standard of proof: the Crown must remove any reasonable doubt that the accused is guilty.
Profound childhood deprivation can reduce moral culpability at sentencing (Bugmy v The Queen, 2013).
The duty to prove the case. In a criminal trial it lies on the prosecution (Woolmington v DPP, 1935).
A state's practical ability to investigate and try crime.
A compulsory pre-committal meeting of prosecution and defence to discuss the evidence and a plea (2018).
The link between the act and the result: the act must be a substantial and operating cause (Royall, 1991).
The warning that the person does not have to say or do anything, and that anything they say may be used in evidence (Evidence Act s 89).
A child cannot be cautioned if cautioned three or more times in the previous three years (YOA s 20(7)).
Rejecting a potential juror for a stated reason, such as bias. No limit.
A non-citizen with a substantial criminal record (12 months or more) fails it; the visa is cancelled automatically while they are in prison (s 501(3A)).
Since 2018, the prosecutor confirms in a certificate, early in the case, the charges that will go ahead.
Also called plea bargaining. Discussions between the prosecution and defence in which the accused agrees to plead guilty to fewer or less serious charges, or to an agreed set of facts.
The rights in the Victims Rights and Support Act 2013 (NSW): to be treated with respect, informed, consulted, heard and supported.
A specialist court, closed to the public, that hears most charges against people under 18 (s 28 CCPA and the Children's Court Act).
A Local Court sentencing process for Aboriginal offenders (since 2002) in which the Local Court judge sits in a circle with Elders, the offender, the victim and lawyers to agree a sentence.
A case with no direct evidence of guilt, where the jury must decide whether guilt is the only rational inference from the facts (Dawson, Patterson).
Facts from which guilt can be inferred, rather than direct proof. Guilt must be the only rational inference.
A case brought by one person for many with the same claim, as in Meredith v NSW.
The share of recorded incidents where legal proceedings began within 90 days (BOCSAR).
Written into an Act by Parliament; doli incapax was codified in s 5 of the CCPA from 1 March 2026.
A course of abusive conduct intended to coerce or control a current or former partner (Crimes Act 1900 s 54D, from 1 July 2024).
A course (pattern) of abusive conduct against a current or former intimate partner, with intent to coerce or control; an offence since 1 July 2024.
The step that sends an indictable case from the Local Court to a higher court for trial or sentence.
Law made by judges in decided cases, such as the rules on causation.
An order of up to 3 years with conditions such as supervision, community service, a curfew or treatment (s 8).
What society needs from the process: protection from crime, offenders brought to justice, compliance with the law, resources used well.
The ICC acts only if a state is unwilling or unable to prosecute (Rome Statute art 17).
A defence that, if it succeeds, leads to an acquittal: self-defence, necessity, duress, automatism, mistake of fact, consent, mental health impairment.
The offences of failing to report a serious indictable offence (s 316) or child abuse (s 316A, 2018) to police.
An order of up to 2 years with good behaviour conditions, with or without a conviction (s 9).
The offence (Crimes Act s 93X) of habitually associating with convicted offenders after an official police warning.
A Supreme Court order detaining a high-risk sex or violent offender after the sentence ends, for up to 5 years, renewable.
Detention in a youth justice centre; the last rung of the ladder (CROC art 37(b): a last resort, for the shortest appropriate time).
A document issued by police stating when and where a person must appear in court and the charge; it has replaced the summons for police prosecutions.
The NSW court that hears appeals against conviction and sentence from the District and Supreme Courts.
An act or omission against the community at large that is punishable by the state.
A leader's planning or launching of an act of aggression that manifestly violates the UN Charter (art 8 bis).
Acts such as murder or torture committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians (art 7).
An on-the-spot fine for a minor offence; under EDDI (2024) a $400 notice for small quantities of a drug, with no conviction.
Questioning of a witness by the opposing side, to test the reliability and credibility of their evidence.
The state as prosecutor, acting for the community; the case is named R (or Rex) v the accused.
The DPP's appeal that a sentence is manifestly inadequate (Criminal Appeal Act 1912 s 5D).
The officer responsible for a person in custody, who must caution them and explain their rights (s 122).
The Aboriginal Legal Service line the custody manager must call whenever an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander person is in custody (mandatory since 2016).
Crime that is never reported, so never recorded or investigated; statistics measure reporting as much as offending.
The court's public condemnation of the conduct on behalf of the community.
Offences that come to light through police activity (drug possession, traffic, offensive conduct) rather than a report, so recorded rates track policing priorities.
A warrant from an authorised officer (magistrate or registrar) extending the investigation period once by up to 6 hours (s 118).
Discouraging crime by the threat of detection or punishment.
An order (LEPRA ss 76AA–76AQ; widened 2026) requiring a person to unlock a device or give passwords.
The independent office that prosecutes indictable offences through Crown prosecutors, and decides charges, plea deals and appeals.
The offence is proved but no conviction is recorded; the offender may be released with or without conditions.
Crime moving to another place or form when one opportunity is blocked.
Dealing with an offender outside court: a warning, caution, youth justice conference or infringement notice.
The part of the Criminal Code (Cth) that makes genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes Australian offences.
The rule that no one should be tried twice for the same offence.
The conduct must be a crime in both states.
The accused's will was overborne by threats of serious harm.
Poverty, unemployment and the cost of living.
Dishonest gain: property, white collar and computer offences, and wage theft.
How well the law achieves its purposes: protecting rights, preventing crime and delivering outcomes society accepts as just.
A choice made by the prosecution or the accused about which court hears a matter.
Making the law work in practice: arrest, trial and punishment.
The principle that both sides should have a fair chance to present their case, which depends on both having skilled representation.
Make a judgement based on criteria; determine the value of.
A guilty plea entered just before the trial starts, after it has been prepared. It earns the smallest discount.
A witness's main account, given before cross-examination. The 2026 Bill would let a recorded police interview be an adult complainant's evidence-in-chief.
The accused's duty to point to some evidence raising a defence; the prosecution must then disprove it beyond reasonable doubt.
The questioning of a witness by the side that called them, using open questions.
Liability for a further crime that a member foresaw as a possible outcome (Miller v The Queen, 2016).
A Supreme Court order supervising a high-risk offender in the community after the sentence ends (Crimes (High Risk Offenders) Act 2006).
Constitution s 51(xxix): lets the Commonwealth legislate to carry out treaties.
The surrender of a person by one state to another for trial or punishment.
Applying to conduct outside Australia.
The deceased's conduct was a serious indictable offence that caused the accused to lose self-control, as an ordinary person might have.
A circumstance that makes crime more likely: psychological, social, economic, political or genetic.
A member of the immediate family of a person who died as a result of the offence.
Taking a sample or print from a person for DNA or fingerprint analysis; intimate (blood) or non-intimate (mouth swab) under the Crimes (Forensic Procedures) Act 2000.
Confiscation of property derived from crime.
A list of further offences the offender admits and asks the court to take into account when sentencing for the main offence; they cannot be prosecuted later.
An adult restorative justice program abolished in 2017 after BOCSAR found no reduction in reoffending.
Evidence not available at the trial that is reliable and highly probative: a ground for retrial after acquittal for a very serious offence (2006).
Discouraging others in the community from offending, by making an example of this offender.
Acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group (Rome Statute art 6).
Evidence of an offender's reputation and conduct. Under the 2026 Act (passed May 2026; it commences by proclamation) it can no longer reduce a sentence for any offence.
A proposed hearing where the judge sets limits on how a vulnerable complainant may be questioned, before they give evidence.
A Court of Criminal Appeal judgment, often on the Attorney-General's application, giving guidance on sentencing for a type of offence.
A reduction in sentence for pleading guilty. Under the 2018 scheme it is 25%, 10% or 5%, depending on when the plea is entered.
25% for a plea in the Local Court before committal; 10% after committal, at least 14 days before trial; 5% later.
Evidence of what someone else said, used to prove it is true. Generally excluded, with exceptions such as admissions.
Since 2022, offences committed long ago are sentenced by today's sentencing patterns, but never above the maximum penalty at the time of the offence.
The proportion of searches or scans that find what they are looking for.
Make a judgement about how well something works, using evidence.
Moving or holding people for exploitation; consent is irrelevant.
A jury that cannot agree. The accused may be retried, or the prosecution discontinued.
The International Criminal Court in The Hague, which tries individuals for the four Rome Statute crimes.
The International Court of Justice, which decides disputes between states; it cannot convict individuals.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (1993 to 2017).
A limit the High Court has found in the Constitution: laws cannot burden political communication more than is reasonably necessary (Jarrett, 2026).
In the accused's absence; the ICC cannot hold such trials.
Evidence a court will not allow, for example a statement taken in breach of s 13.
Protecting the community by removing the offender's ability to offend, usually by imprisonment.
A serious offence heard in the District or Supreme Court, usually by a jury.
What the process must protect: privacy, silence, due process, freedom from arbitrary detention, the presumption of innocence, freedom of movement and assembly.
A judicial inquiry into a conviction under the Crimes (Appeal and Review) Act 2001, the route that freed Folbigg.
A trial in which the judge directs the investigation, questions witnesses and builds the case from a written dossier (France, Germany).
Weighing all the relevant factors together to reach one sentence, rather than starting from a number and adding or subtracting (Markarian v The Queen, 2005).
A prison sentence of up to 2 years served in the community under supervision, home detention, monitoring or community service (s 7). Community safety is paramount (s 66).
The time after arrest in which police may detain a person to investigate the offence: a reasonable time up to 6 hours (LEPRA s 115).
Detention of a terrorism suspect aged 14+ for questioning: 4 days, up to 14 with a judge's warrant (Part 2AA).
An agreement to commit a crime; each member is liable for crimes within its scope.
A trial without a jury, on the accused's application. Ordered if the prosecution agrees, or if the court finds it in the interests of justice.
The judge's freedom to fit the sentence to the offence and the offender, within the limits Parliament sets.
Guidance from the courts: guideline judgments, Court of Criminal Appeal decisions and Judicial Commission sentencing statistics.
Courts deciding cases free from direction by Parliament or the executive; mandatory sentences and Kable-type laws test it.
The power of a court to hear a case. Original jurisdiction: to hear a case for the first time. Appellate jurisdiction: to review a lower court's decision.
Whether the matter is a type Legal Aid funds.
A juror acting outside their role, for example making their own inquiries about the case. An offence under Jury Act s 68C (up to 2 years).
Twelve citizens, chosen at random from the electoral roll, who decide the facts and the verdict in a trial of an indictable offence.
Moving money from prison to prevention in the communities most affected.
A court must not impose imprisonment unless satisfied no other penalty is appropriate (s 5).
An independent body that reviews the law and recommends reform; its Report 133 (2012) led to the Bail Act 2013.
The principle in s 7 that criminal proceedings are used only if no alternative is appropriate.
The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (2016): investigates and reports on police misconduct but cannot prosecute.
The government body that funds or provides lawyers for people who cannot afford one, under the Legal Aid Commission Act 1979 (NSW).
Formal action against a suspect: a court attendance notice, charge or youth justice conference.
Having a lawyer (a solicitor, and for trials usually a barrister) to advise, negotiate and speak for you in court.
The Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW): the Act that contains most police powers and the responsibilities that go with them.
The judicial officer of the Local Court. Formally titled 'judge' since 2026; the syllabus still uses 'magistrate'. Decides guilt and sentence alone.
A verdict of 11–1 or 10–1, allowed after at least 8 hours of deliberation if the court is satisfied a unanimous verdict is unlikely (2006).
A person (teacher, doctor, police officer) who must report a child at risk of significant harm.
A penalty Parliament fixes, such as a mandatory minimum, which the court must impose regardless of the offender's circumstances.
So lenient that it falls outside the range a reasonable judge could impose: an error in itself.
The most severe sentence the law allows for an offence, set in the Act that creates the offence. Reserved for the worst cases; a yardstick for the rest.
Whether the applicant's income and assets are low enough to qualify for legal aid.
The mental element: the fault the accused had. In order: intention, recklessness, criminal negligence.
A defence under s 28 of the Mental Health and Cognitive Impairment Forensic Provisions Act 2020 (NSW) when the accused could not reason about wrongfulness.
Whether the case is likely to succeed. Usually applied only to criminal appeals, not trials.
Data about communications (who, when, where) rather than their content; telcos must keep it for two years (Cth, 2015).
Set at 10 in NSW; the ACT raised it to 14 from 1 July 2025.
A circumstance that reduces the offender's culpability or justifies a lighter sentence (s 21A(3)): no prior convictions, remorse, a guilty plea, good prospects of rehabilitation.
Hiding the criminal origin of money.
Help between states in gathering evidence.
The accused broke the law to avoid a greater harm.
The judge's role in the adversary system: to make sure the rules are followed, not to find the evidence.
Since 1 July 2026 a child can receive a caution or conference by not denying the offence, rather than admitting it.
The minimum time an offender must spend in prison before parole can be considered.
A new, independent act that breaks the chain of causation.
A body (2003) that advises the Attorney-General on sentencing law and reform.
Rules for NSW prosecutors: charges must reasonably reflect the criminality and give the court enough sentencing power, and victims and police must be consulted.
Conduct that harms the body or safety of another, such as homicide, assault and coercive control.
Conduct that threatens the state, such as treason, espionage and foreign interference.
Courts sit in public and give reasons, so the community can see justice done.
Crime is more likely when a motivated offender meets a suitable target with no capable guardian.
Aboriginal people are about 3.4% of the NSW population but over 30% of prisoners.
Conditional release from prison after the non-parole period, under supervision; breach returns the person to custody.
A defence to murder only. If it succeeds, the accused is convicted of manslaughter instead: extreme provocation, substantial impairment, excessive self-defence, infanticide.
A person who runs a case in court. The prosecution and the accused are parties; the victim is not.
The school's criteria: Protection of individual rights, Enforceability, Accessibility, Resource efficiency, Responsiveness, Justice achieved, Application of the rule of law, Meeting society's needs.
An on-the-spot fine for a minor offence, without going to court.
The unit fines are set in: $110 in NSW.
Moving people across a border illegally for payment, usually with their consent.
Rejecting a potential juror without giving a reason. Each side has three.
An order that a trial will not go ahead because it would be an abuse of process.
The accused's formal answer to a charge in court: guilty or not guilty.
The freedom police have to choose whether and how to use a power: investigate, search, arrest, charge, divert, grant bail.
A crime of taking steps towards an offence not yet committed: attempt, conspiracy, preparation.
A person is treated as innocent until proven guilty; remand is the clearest exception in practice.
A court order holding a person aged 16+ for up to 14 days to prevent an imminent terrorist act or preserve evidence (Part 2A).
The person against whom the offence was committed.
The person who commits the criminal act.
A person present who aids, abets or encourages the crime.
A prosecution started by a private person rather than by police or the DPP.
A fair process: each side is heard, and the rules are applied equally. It becomes substantive justice only if the sides are evenly matched.
The sentence must fit the seriousness of the crime; it cannot be increased beyond that to protect the community (Veen (No 2), 1988).
The prosecutor's choice about which charges to lay, accept, change or withdraw.
Separating inmates at risk from other prisoners, such as former police, informants and sex offenders.
Mental illness, impairment, addiction and trauma.
Independent senior barristers, paid by the State, who defend legally aided accused in serious trials and appeals.
The process by which a person comes to support violent extremism, often online.
Software that locks or steals data until a payment is made.
The only force police may use to arrest (LEPRA s 231); excessive force is assault or, if death results, manslaughter.
More than a possibility, less than a belief, with some factual basis; judged on what the officer knew at the time (R v Rondo, 2001).
The second step of s 99: arrest must be needed for a listed reason (stop the offence, stop flight, establish identity, ensure court attendance, preserve evidence, protect safety).
A presumption that applies unless the Crown proves otherwise, as doli incapax does for a child aged 10 to 13.
Reoffending after a sentence. About half of people released from NSW prisons return within two years.
Using a child to commit a crime; an offence from June 2026 (s 351A).
An INTERPOL request to locate and provisionally arrest a person; not an arrest warrant.
A person convicted of a child sex offence who must report to police under the Child Protection (Offenders Registration) Act 2000.
Changing the offender so they do not reoffend, through treatment, education or supervision.
Custody awaiting trial or sentence; the person has not been convicted.
Wood CJ at CL suggested children convicted of murder be resentenced at about 21; NSW has not adopted it.
How quickly and fully the law adapts to new problems.
Bringing the offender, the victim and the community together to repair the harm, rather than only to punish.
Punishment the offender deserves, in proportion to the crime.
An exception where the accused must prove something, on the balance of probabilities: mental health impairment, substantial impairment, 'show cause' at bail.
A suspect need not answer police questions, and silence cannot be treated as evidence of guilt (Evidence Act s 89); s 89A (2013) is the exception.
Everyone, including the State, is bound by and equal before the law, applied by independent courts.
Evidence Act: improperly or illegally obtained evidence is excluded unless the desirability of admitting it outweighs the undesirability.
A legal condition on a power that protects the individual: s 201 (name, place of duty, reason), reasonable force (s 231), a warrant, a support person.
Asset freezes and travel bans imposed by a government on a person or body.
The Sexual Assault Reporting Option: adults can give police information online without starting a formal investigation.
A serious children's indictable offence, such as murder or (since September 2026) shooting at a building; dealt with according to law in the District or Supreme Court (s 17).
Examining a person, vehicle or premises for evidence (LEPRA s 21 on reasonable suspicion) and taking what is found.
A document from a magistrate or authorised officer authorising police to enter and search premises and seize things (LEPRA Part 5).
The discretion to exclude improperly or illegally obtained evidence unless the desirability of admitting it outweighs the undesirability of how it was obtained.
No conviction can be recorded for a child under 16; the court may refuse to record one for a 16 or 17-year-old.
Makes it an offence to publish a child's name in a way that identifies them.
The youth bail test (2024): for 14 to 17-year-olds charged with serious break and enter or car theft while on bail, refuse unless there is a 'high degree of confidence' they will not reoffend.
Lists the penalties the Children's Court can impose, from dismissal to a control order of up to 2 years for one offence.
From 1 July 2026 a non-denial statement is inadmissible as evidence in later proceedings.
Corrective Services' assessment of the risk an inmate poses, from minimum to maximum security, which decides where they are held and what they may do.
The criticism that only some offenders, from weaker states, are tried.
The accused believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another, and it was a reasonable response as they saw the situation.
A court order (2016) restricting a person's associations, movement and internet use for up to 5 years; interim orders (2026) let police impose restrictions before the hearing.
Wrong in a moral sense, not merely naughty or against the law (RP v The Queen, 2016).
An offender's appeal that the sentence is too severe.
For listed serious offences the accused must show why their detention is not justified, or bail must be refused (Bail Act s 16A, 2014).
Making crime harder, riskier or less rewarding in a particular place: cameras, lighting, locks, scanning.
Family, peers, education and community.
Tackling the causes of offending, such as disadvantage, before crime happens.
The intent to destroy a group, which separates genocide from other crimes.
'Act proven but not criminally responsible': the mental health impairment verdict.
Discouraging this offender from reoffending.
A guidepost for mid-range offences; the 20-year SNPP for murder did not apply to CL because he was a juvenile.
The non-parole period Parliament sets for an offence in the middle of the range of seriousness: a guidepost, not a starting point (Muldrock, 2011).
How convincingly the case must be proved. Criminal: beyond reasonable doubt (Evidence Act s 141). Civil: the balance of probabilities.
The body that decides parole for sentences over three years, with community safety paramount.
A state that has ratified a treaty; the Rome Statute has 125.
A foreign state body listed under the 2025 Act for directing or supporting terrorism.
An Act of Parliament, such as the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW).
Limits set by Parliament: maximum penalties, standard non-parole periods, mandatory sentences, and the purposes (s 3A) and factors (s 21A) in the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999.
A court order pausing or stopping a trial, for example until an unrepresented accused is represented (Dietrich).
The Suspect Targeting Management Plan, a police program that rates people by risk of offending; criticised for how many young Aboriginal people it lists.
An offence for which only the act must be proved, without mens rea.
An offence that must go to a higher court, such as murder.
A search requiring removal of clothing; outside a station only where serious and urgent, never under 10 (LEPRA ss 31–34).
An abnormality of mind from an underlying condition substantially impaired the accused's capacity. The accused must prove it.
A minor offence heard in the Local Court by a judge alone.
An older document, issued by a registrar, requiring attendance at court; still used in private prosecutions.
A parent or responsible person, or from age 14 an adult the child chooses or their lawyer; must be present for the child's interview.
Money or property pledged by the accused or another person that is forfeited if the accused fails to appear.
An indictable offence dealt with in the Local Court unless the prosecution or the accused elects a higher court.
An indictable offence dealt with in the Local Court unless the prosecution elects a higher court.
An acquittal obtained through an offence such as perjury or jury tampering.
Time not counted in the investigation period: waiting for a lawyer, interpreter or support person; medical treatment; rest; travel (s 117).
Make a judgement about how far something is true, supported by evidence.
Crime that crosses borders in its commission, planning, organisation or effects (UNTOC art 3(2)).
The main test (s 17): will the accused fail to appear, commit a serious offence, endanger safety, or interfere with witnesses or evidence?
The test the court applies at every bail decision: whether the accused is an unacceptable risk of failing to appear, committing a serious offence, endangering safety or interfering with witnesses.
All twelve jurors agree.
The UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime (2000).
The practical benefit of a guilty plea: it saves court time and money, spares victims and witnesses a trial, and makes a conviction certain.
The power of a permanent member of the UN Security Council to block a decision.
Before the court takes negotiated charges or facts into account, the prosecutor must certify that the victim and police were consulted. It is consultation, not a veto.
A statement by a primary victim, or a family member in a homicide case, describing the physical, emotional and financial harm (ss 26–30A).
A register through which victims are told about an offender's parole, release and escape.
Counselling, financial assistance and recognition payments for victims of violent crime.
A hearing within the trial, without the jury, to decide whether evidence is admissible.
A child, a person with impaired intellectual functioning, an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander person, or a person with limited English, who must have a support person (LEPRA Regulation).
Intentional underpayment of wages, a crime from 1 January 2025 (Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) s 327A).
A District Court list (2022) in which Elders lead the sentencing conversation for Aboriginal adults, with a monitored plan.
Scanning a person with a hand-held metal detector in a declared area without a warrant or suspicion (2024, permanent 2026).
Serious violations of the laws of armed conflict (art 8).
The lightest tier: a police officer tells the child the conduct is wrong. No record is kept as a criminal record.
Leaving a treaty; under the Rome Statute it takes effect a year after notice (art 127).
People who fail the means test but still cannot afford a private lawyer.
A proposed order (bill, October 2026) excluding abusive customers from a workplace.
A detention centre for children; a person sentenced to a SCIO term may begin it there (s 19).
A restorative conference for young offenders under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (Part 5).
A court process (Practice Note 11) for Aboriginal children in the Children's Court, with Elders and an Action and Support Plan; sits at three sites.
In Australian law, the union of two people to the exclusion of all others, voluntarily entered into for life.
A relationship between two people who live together as a couple on a genuine domestic basis and are not married to each other.
A family formed when a couple live together with children from earlier relationships.
The system of family relationships and obligations that connects Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people to each other, to community and to Country.
A marriage that has no legal effect, for example because one person was already married or did not give real consent.
All the duties, powers, responsibilities and authority that parents have by law in relation to their children.
The paramount consideration a court must apply when it makes a parenting order.
The legal process that permanently transfers parental rights and responsibilities from the birth parents to the adoptive parents.
A written, signed and dated agreement between parents about the care of their children. It is not enforceable by a court.
A court order about who a child lives with, spends time with and communicates with, and who makes major decisions.
Money paid by a parent towards the cost of raising a child after separation.
The legal ending of a marriage by a court order.
The only ground for divorce in Australia, shown by 12 months of separation.
The division of the assets and debts of a couple after separation.
A written agreement between partners, made with independent legal advice, about how property will be divided if they separate.
A court order that restricts a person's behaviour to protect someone they have a domestic relationship with.
A process in which an independent practitioner helps separating families to agree, usually required before applying for a parenting order.
A pattern of abusive behaviour used to control or dominate an intimate partner.
An arrangement in which a woman agrees to carry a child for another person or couple who will become the child's parents.
Surrogacy in which the birth mother receives no payment beyond her reasonable costs.
A court order that transfers legal parentage of a child from the birth mother to the intended parents after surrogacy.
The legal duty of certain workers, such as teachers and doctors, to report a child at risk of significant harm.
Care for a child who cannot live safely at home, such as foster care or kinship care.
Basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person because they are human. They are universal, inherent, inalienable and indivisible.
Describes rights that cannot be taken or given away.
The right of all adult citizens to vote, whatever their sex, race or wealth.
The right of a people to decide their own political status and to pursue their own economic, social and cultural development.
Rights held by a group of people rather than by one person, such as self-determination, environmental rights and peace rights.
An organisation of workers formed to protect and improve pay and conditions.
The 1948 declaration of the United Nations General Assembly that first set out the rights all people should have. It is not a binding treaty.

gloss.term: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
gloss.def: The 1966 treaty that binds states to protect rights such as life, liberty, a fair trial, free speech and the vote.

gloss.term: International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
gloss.def: The 1966 treaty that binds states to work towards rights such as work, health, education and an adequate standard of living.
The name given to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the two 1966 covenants together.
The authority of a state to govern itself and make its own laws without outside interference.
A written agreement between states that is binding in international law on the states that ratify it.
The step by which a state formally agrees to be bound by a treaty.
An organisation whose members are states, set up by treaty, such as the United Nations or the Commonwealth of Nations.
The United Nations body responsible for international peace and security. Its five permanent members each hold a veto.
The main court of the United Nations. It hears disputes between states and gives advisory opinions.
The United Nations body of 47 member states that reviews the human rights record of every member state.
A legal system in which a treaty has no effect in domestic law until parliament passes legislation to enact it.
Rights written into the Australian Constitution, such as freedom of religion in s 116.
Rights that the High Court has found are implied by the text and structure of the Constitution, such as the freedom of political communication.
A document that lists the rights a government must respect. Australia has none at the national level.
The independent national body that investigates and conciliates complaints of discrimination and breaches of human rights, and reports to parliament.
A place to live that gives protection, privacy and security.
Housing that is secure, affordable, habitable, accessible and in a suitable location, as described in international law.
Rental housing provided by the government or community organisations for people on low incomes.
Premises where residents rent a room, not the whole dwelling, and share facilities.
Ownership of a unit or lot in a building, together with a share in the common property.
The system in which the government keeps a register of land ownership and guarantees the title shown on it.
The sale of a property at a price negotiated between the seller and the buyer.
A public sale in which the property is sold to the highest bidder, with no cooling-off period.
A short time after contracts are exchanged in which a buyer can withdraw from a private treaty sale.
A loan secured over land. The lender can sell the property if the borrower defaults.
"Let the buyer beware": the buyer is responsible for checking the property before buying.
The legal work of transferring ownership of land from the seller to the buyer.
The point at which the buyer and the seller swap signed contracts and the sale becomes binding.
A lease: a contract in which a landlord lets a tenant live in a property in return for rent.
Money paid by a tenant at the start of a lease as security, lodged with NSW Fair Trading.
A record of the state of a rented property at the start of a tenancy.
A written notice from a landlord or a tenant that ends a tenancy on a stated date.
The tribunal that hears most tenancy, strata and home building disputes in NSW.
A tenant's confidence that they can stay in their home as long as they meet their obligations.
The relationship between housing costs and household income.
Often defined as a lower-income household spending more than 30 per cent of its income on housing.
Having no home, or living in housing that is inadequate, insecure or without control over one's own space.
Short-term emergency housing for people who have nowhere safe to stay.
The process of changing the law so that it better meets the needs and values of society.
An independent body that reviews areas of law and recommends changes to the government.
A major public inquiry, set up by the government, with strong powers to gather evidence.
An organisation that campaigns to influence public opinion and the law on an issue.
The removal of a law by parliament.
A change made to an existing law or to a bill.
The process by which courts work out the meaning of the words in an Act.
"Land belonging to no one": the doctrine, rejected in 1992, that Australia had no owners before British settlement.
The recognition in Australian law of the rights and interests of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples in land and waters under their traditional laws and customs.
Rights to land granted to Aboriginal people by legislation, such as the Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1983 (NSW).
A body set up under NSW legislation that can claim certain Crown land and manage it for Aboriginal people.
The ending of native title, for example by a grant of freehold land.
Australia's independent regulator for online safety.
Methods used to check or estimate the age of a person using an online service.
A social media service that Australian law requires to take reasonable steps to stop people under 16 from holding accounts.
The party that brings a criminal case against an accused person on behalf of the state.
A person charged with a criminal offence.
The principle that an accused person is treated as innocent until proved guilty.
The standard of proof in a criminal case.
A less serious offence heard by a magistrate in the Local Court.
A serious offence usually tried by a judge and jury.
A penalty imposed by a court on a person found guilty of an offence.
The person who starts a civil case.
In a civil case, the person who is being sued.
The standard of proof in a civil case: more likely than not.
A civil wrong, other than a breach of contract, for which the law provides a remedy.
A failure to take reasonable care that causes harm to a person to whom a duty of care is owed.
A legal obligation to avoid acts or omissions that could reasonably be foreseen to harm others.
A legally binding agreement between two or more parties.
Money awarded by a court to compensate a plaintiff for loss.
A court order that requires a person to do, or to stop doing, something.
The area of law that deals with the decisions and actions of government bodies and officials.
A court's review of whether a government decision was made lawfully.
A fresh look at a government decision by a tribunal, which can change the decision.
A body that resolves certain disputes with less cost and formality than a court.
An independent official who investigates complaints about government agencies.
Ways of settling a dispute without a court hearing, such as negotiation, mediation and conciliation.
A process in which a neutral third person helps the parties reach their own agreement.
The idea that children gain the ability to make their own decisions as they mature.
The age below which a child cannot be charged with a criminal offence: 10 in NSW.
The presumption that a child aged 10 to under 14 does not know that their conduct is seriously wrong.
Reoffending after being dealt with by the criminal justice system.
Dealing with an offender, especially a young person, outside the formal court process.
A meeting in which a young offender, the victim and others agree on a plan to repair the harm.

gloss.term: Convention on the Rights of the Child
gloss.def: The 1989 treaty that sets out the rights of everyone under 18.
A person who has left their country and applied for protection as a refugee, and whose claim has not yet been decided.
A person outside their country who has a well-founded fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a particular social group.
The duty not to return a person to a place where they face persecution or serious harm.
The legal requirement that a non-citizen in Australia without a valid visa be detained.
The assessment of asylum claims in a country other than the one where protection is sought.
A visa granted to a person in Australia who is found to be owed protection.
A set of rules made by the state that binds everyone in the community and is enforced by the courts.
The principle that everyone, including the government, is subject to the law and equal before it.
The fair and impartial treatment of all people under the law.
The right to a fair hearing by an unbiased decision-maker.
Law that governs the relationship between individuals and the state, such as criminal and constitutional law.
Law that governs relationships between individuals, such as contract and tort law.
The absence of law and government.
Law made by judges through their decisions in cases.
Law made by parliament.
A court decision that guides or binds later courts deciding similar cases.
The legal reason for a court's decision, which forms the binding precedent.
Remarks made by a judge in passing that are not binding but may be persuasive.
The principle that courts stand by what has already been decided.
A proposed law that has not yet been passed by parliament.
The formal approval of a bill by the Governor-General or a Governor, which makes it an Act.
Rules made by a body that parliament has given the power to make them, such as regulations and by-laws.
The power of a court to hear a particular kind of matter.
The power of a court to hear a case for the first time.
The power of a court to hear appeals from lower courts.
A system of trial in which two opposing sides present their cases to an impartial judge or jury.
The way the Constitution shares law-making power between the Commonwealth and the states.
The division of government into the legislature, the executive and the judiciary so that no one body holds all power.
Law-making powers that only the Commonwealth Parliament can use.
Law-making powers shared by the Commonwealth and the states.
Law-making powers left with the states because the Constitution does not give them to the Commonwealth.
A national vote on a proposal to change the Constitution.
The laws, customs and practices of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, passed on by word of mouth, story, song and ceremony.
A respected senior member of an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander community who holds and passes on knowledge and Lore.
The lands, waters and skies to which Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples are connected.
Rules that bind states because states follow them consistently out of a sense of legal duty.
A political unit with a defined territory, a permanent population, a government and the capacity to deal with other states.
Being held in custody while waiting for a trial or sentence.
A trial for an indictable offence in which a judge, without a jury, decides the verdict.
A program that directs an offender away from the usual court or prison path and into treatment, education or support.
The level of security, such as maximum, medium or minimum, at which a prisoner is held.
A Supreme Court order that keeps a high-risk offender under strict supervision in the community after their sentence ends.
A Supreme Court order that keeps a high-risk offender in custody after their sentence ends.
The minimum time an offender must spend in custody before being eligible for release on parole.
The ways nation-states and international organisations deal with each other, including through diplomacy, trade, law and conflict.
The management of relations between states by negotiation.
A treaty between three or more states.
A treaty between two states.
The growing connection of countries through trade, technology, travel and communication.

gloss.term: United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
gloss.def: The 2007 declaration that sets out the individual and collective rights of Indigenous peoples. It is not a binding treaty.
A marriage entered into without the free and full consent of one or both people, because of coercion, threat or deception, or where a person is under 16.
Care of a child in the home of an authorised carer when the child cannot live safely with their parents.

gloss.term: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Child Placement Principle
gloss.def: The principle that an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander child who cannot live at home should be placed, in order of priority, with family, community or other Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander carers.
Land and anything fixed to it, such as a house.
Social housing managed by not-for-profit organisations.
Social housing owned and managed by the state government.
A funded service that gives accommodation and support to people who are homeless or at risk of homelessness.

tf.t: A crime is an act or omission against the community that is punishable by the state.
Actus reus is the physical element of a crime.
tf.f: Actus reus is the mental element of a crime.

tf.t: Recklessness can satisfy the mental element of an offence.
Indictable offences are usually tried by a judge and jury in a higher court.
tf.f: Indictable offences are finalised by a magistrate sitting alone.

tf.t: The prosecution must prove actus reus and mens rea, not motive.
tf.f: Motive is an element the prosecution must always prove.

tf.t: Criminal negligence can amount to mens rea for some offences, such as manslaughter.
Police can arrest without a warrant if they suspect on reasonable grounds that a person has committed an offence and the arrest is reasonably necessary.
Bail is the conditional release of an accused person until the case is heard.
tf.f: Bail means the accused has been found not guilty.

tf.t: An accused who is refused bail is held on remand.
Police can search without a warrant in some situations, such as on reasonable suspicion.
tf.f: Police need a warrant for every search.

tf.t: A court attendance notice tells an accused when and where to appear in court.
A person on remand has not been convicted and is presumed innocent.
tf.f: A person on remand has been convicted.

tf.t: The burden of proof in a criminal trial rests on the prosecution.
The Director of Public Prosecutions prosecutes serious offences on behalf of the state.
tf.f: The Director of Public Prosecutions represents the accused.

tf.t: Public Defenders are barristers who represent people who have been granted legal aid in serious matters.
A magistrate sits alone, without a jury.
tf.f: A magistrate sits with a jury in the Local Court.

tf.t: The Court of Criminal Appeal hears appeals against conviction and sentence from the District and Supreme Courts.
The accused cannot be forced to give evidence.
tf.f: The accused must give evidence at their trial.

tf.t: Imprisonment is a sentence of last resort in NSW.
A guideline judgment is issued by the Court of Criminal Appeal to guide sentencing for an offence.
tf.f: A guideline judgment is a law passed by parliament.

tf.t: The prosecution can appeal against a sentence it considers manifestly inadequate.
A fine is a non-custodial penalty.
tf.f: A fine is a custodial sentence.

tf.t: A standard non-parole period guides the court when it sentences for certain serious offences.
The maximum penalty is reserved for the worst cases.
tf.f: The maximum penalty must be given for every offence.

tf.t: A child under 10 cannot be charged with a criminal offence in NSW.
The Children's Court is a closed court.
tf.f: The Children's Court is open to the public.

tf.t: Detention is a last resort for young offenders.
Penalties for children are set out in the Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW).
tf.f: A young offender is sentenced under the same Act as an adult.

tf.t: The Convention on the Rights of the Child says the best interests of the child must be a primary consideration.
The International Criminal Court was set up by the Rome Statute.
The International Criminal Court tries individuals.
tf.f: The International Criminal Court tries countries rather than people.

tf.t: Extradition is the surrender of a person by one state to another to face trial or punishment.
Transnational crimes are prosecuted under the domestic law of the states involved.
tf.f: Transnational crimes can only be prosecuted by international courts.

tf.t: State sovereignty can limit the enforcement of international criminal law.
A marriage is void if one person was already legally married to someone else.
De facto relationships are also recognised by the law.
tf.f: A couple must be married for the law to recognise their relationship.

tf.t: Both parents have parental responsibility for a child unless a court orders otherwise.
A court considers the child's views, giving them weight according to the child's age and maturity.
tf.f: Children have no say in parenting disputes.

tf.t: A marriage celebrant must be authorised under the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth).
Australia has had no-fault divorce since the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) began.
They can, but they must usually attend counselling first or get the court's permission.
tf.f: A couple married for less than two years cannot divorce.

tf.t: Non-financial contributions, such as caring for children, count in a property settlement.
Police can and often must apply on the victim's behalf.
tf.f: Only the victim can apply for an apprehended domestic violence order.

tf.t: Breaching an apprehended domestic violence order is a criminal offence.
A parenting plan is not legally enforceable; a parenting order is.
tf.f: A parenting plan is enforceable in the same way as a court order.

tf.t: Same-sex couples have been able to marry in Australia since December 2017.

items.samp: Students will present statements that demonstrate the extent to which the operation of the courts achieve justice for individuals, victims, offenders, society, or all of these within the criminal justice system. Statements may include: Nature of crime in relation to serious and indictable offences – courts are the only vehicle In the eyes of society, courts reflect this notion of justice being achieved – removal from society etc. Punishment and sentencing decisions and processes are an indicator of justice, eg Sentencing guidelines, VIS, Truth in Sentencing Official process, formal delivery Adversarial nature and system which is a mechanism for justice Primary agents for common law – significant part that delivers justice Provision of legal aid enables access to the court system to provide for justice Appellate structure of the court structure Use of evidence and rules of admissibility Role of juries, eg reform of jury system Cater for special groups – young offenders, coroners court, drug court – relating to specific or ‘special’ issues, as well as using closed courts with cases of a special nature Protections offered by the burden of proof and standard of proof – much higher in a criminal case Court processes probe deeper into an issue to determine and identify facts Nature of crime – alternative forms of punishment issued to a variety of crimes that don’t require the use of courts Role of discretion outside the court system can deliver justice, eg police discretion Court processes are lengthy and expensive Geographical isolation – can’t access specific court’s use of community mediation, circle sentencing, re-integrative shaming. Negotiation of punishment from ADR might affect justice in greater terms than in a court, eg 50 hours of community service versus a caution issued in a court Legal aid is not guaranteed to all – criteria based Measure of success depends on the quality of legal representation Plea and charge negotiation in some instances is not viewed as an adequate punishment if entered into Public nature of courts prejudice the outcome if subject to media exposure eg trial by media Remove juries and have a specialised panel of experts to make decisions eg admissibility of DNA or issues relying on medical expertise VIS can sway punishment outcomes Role of media in court process, eg video statements of victims not enabling cross examination Not inquisitorial, can’t get into all the facts Outcome based on the rules of the court Disproportionate impact on lower socioeconomic groups, eg traffic fines

items.samp: Some contemporary issues are listed in the Legal Studies syllabus in dot point 3 of Human Rights. This is not an exhaustive list. Points against state sovereignty enforcing human rights would be expected to dominate in responses. These points include: States can ignore international human rights statements. States can enact discriminatory laws and engage in repressive practices. States can remove existing domestic human rights protections. States can ignore domestic human rights violations. Points for state sovereignty enforcing human rights include: States can exercise influence in international forums. States can impose sanctions on other states for breaches of human rights. items.samp: Reference to human rights legislation or referenda. A charter of rights is the document that sets out a country’s or group of people’s human rights and entitlements within a nation state. There are many reasons for and/or against Australia adopting a charter of rights. Within Australia the extent to which human rights would be protected would depend upon the way in which a charter of rights was created. If it is a legislated charter of rights, it is one created by parliament. The effect this has on the protection of human rights is that it is at the will of the parliament. This means that the human rights afforded can be changed at any time. On the other hand a legislative charter of rights provides for a uniform and codified method of protection. On the other hand, if it is a constitutional charter of rights the effects on human rights would be protected differently. This type of charter provides, to some extent, a better level of protection as it is one that is difficult to change. In order to change this charter a nation state needs to implement a referendum. This is time consuming, costly and not always successful.

It also protects an individual’s freedom of religion from government interference. The Constitution also provides an accused person the right to trial by jury for serious offences. The separation of powers between the judiciary, legislature and executive, as outlined in the Constitution, protects individuals against the arbitrary exercise of government power.

items.samp: The role of international courts is to protect human rights by prosecuting those who commit grave breaches of human rights. International courts can only prosecute offenders if they are not dealt with by courts in the country they reside in, or if the country allows the court to do so. The International Criminal Court (ICC), established in 2002 by the Rome Statute, has successfully tried some people accused of violating human rights, however the first success, the Lubanga case in 2012, took 10 years and cost millions of dollars. In total since its establishment the ICC has two convictions – Lubanga in 2012 and Katanga in 2014. This shows that whilst they are successful in protecting human rights, international courts are time consuming and need a lot of resources to secure a conviction. Domestic courts also prosecute those who have allegedly breached human rights, but cover a wider range of human rights abuses and are less time and resource consuming than international courts. This can be seen in the R v Wei Tang case in 2008 where it took less than a year for the High Court to uphold the conviction for slavery. However, in countries without legislation banning human rights abuses, offenders may not be prosecuted in domestic courts but may actually be protected from prosecution. If an offender is a person in power, they may be protected from prosecution in both international and domestic courts.

items.samp: Law reform has been effective in the movement towards the abolition of slavery. The move to abolish slavery began in the 12th century. The transatlantic slave trade gradually gave way to changing social values and led to law reform to protect individual rights. In addition, France abolished slavery in 1794 and there was a worldwide movement towards abolishing slavery. In the USA, the US Constitution was amended to abolish slavery. This is an example of domestic law reform responding to changing community standards. Slavery was the first human rights issue to raise wide international concern. The Slavery Convention (1926) was the first document to prohibit slavery, with a number of countries ratifying this convention. There was further law reform under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) (1948) and International Convention on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) (1966). Despite efforts at law reform, slavery still exists in a number of countries. – 2 –

items.samp: A number of important rights have been developed by the common law. For example, Dietrich v The Queen (1992) recognised the importance of a fair trial through the provision of legal aid to the accused in a serious criminal matter. Similarly, statute law has made an important contribution to the enforcement of human rights. Legislation such as the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) and Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) enshrine principles that reflect community values and set standards in the enforcement of human rights. Common law and statute law are similar as they both work together to enforce and protect human rights. Mabo v Queensland (1992) protected indigenous land rights, which then required parliament to pass legislation. Also, both are capable of responding to change and protect the same rights, such as freedom from discrimination. Common law and statute law differ in some ways. For example, common law evolves on a case-by-case basis over time whereas statute law is modified based on a range of factors. They also differ in that common law is made by judges and statute law is made by parliament. – 3 –

items.samp: A Charter of Rights is a legal document which sets out the civil and political rights of citizens in a country. Many people argue that Australia needs to protect the most vulnerable citizens in society, for example homeless people, refugees and Indigenous people. It is easier to access these rights from one source such as a Charter of Rights. This is a reason why Australia should have a Charter of Rights. On the other hand, we have a vibrant democracy in Australia and therefore do not need a Charter of Rights. Although it represents current values of our society, when it is written, these values can become outdated, eg the US right to bear arms. Listing rights may limit them. A Charter of Rights entrenched in the Constitution is difficult to change whereas a statutory Charter of Rights is easier to change. – 2 –

items.samp: Human rights are protected by both international and domestic law. However, sometimes these laws are not adequately enforced in practice meaning that human rights legal protection is limited. The example of asylum seekers coming to Australia shows that, although the law aims to protect human rights, this is not always the reality. Under international law people have the right to seek asylum: Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Refugee Convention (1951) to which Australia is a signatory. Under the doctrines of state sovereignty, a nation also has the right to make its own laws according to the values of its citizens. Under the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) Australia has a system of mandatory detention often in offshore locations for those who arrive by boat without a valid visa. The High Court has said that the law made by Parliament about offshore detention is valid. Although international law protects asylum seekers in theory, the doctrine of state sovereignty allows Australia to circumvent this protection and thus limit the enforcement of human rights. – 3 –

items.samp: Human rights are protected by both legal and non-legal measures. However, these legal and non-legal measures are not always as effective as each other. The effectiveness of legal and non-legal measures is based both on raising awareness in the community about the importance of the issue, and also promoting change in the community to ensure positive outcomes for the future. A contemporary issue that has been discussed in the community is the treatment of young people in detention. Under the Convention on the Rights of Children, a treaty to which Australia is a signatory, incarceration should only be used as a last resort and the rehabilitation of young offenders should be a priority eg Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW). The media plays an important role in promoting human rights for young people. The publicity given to the treatment of young people a the Don Dale Detention Centre in the Northern Territory led to the establishment of a Royal Commission into the treatment of young people in detention. This shows that non-legal measures can have a significant influence on legal measures in our society. The detention of minors in adult prisons in Victoria has also been the subject of media attention that has forced administrative changes in that state. – 3 –

items.samp: Separation of powers is written into Australia’s Constitution, and divides power between the executive, legislature and judiciary. It means that no one arm of the government has too much power and allows for checks and balances eg no political party or member of the government can interfere with the decisions made by a judge or magistrate. This is important to avoid the arbitrary abuse of power and to uphold the rule of law. Both the legislature and the judiciary can make laws to protect human rights eg the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW) limits the powers of the executive (police) and in Dietrich v The Queen (1992) the High Court judges protected the right to legal representation. Separation of powers enables people to challenge laws made by the parliament in court if they believe the law contravenes their human rights eg Mabo v Queensland (1992). Separation of powers protects human rights by ensuring that no one is above the law and providing fairness and access to the law.

items.samp: Non-government organisations (NGOs) and the media can be very effective tools in the promotion of human rights. Human rights abuses are brought to the attention of the world in the media and through NGOs such as Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch. Amnesty International is effective in reporting on human rights abuses to the United Nations. But NGOs rely heavily on support from donations and volunteers. Their efforts can be hindered by countries denying access to war-torn areas. Media coverage is a very powerful tool in the promotion of human rights. The media can name and shame governments eg to get people to pressure their government to act. Social media platforms spread awareness and expose abuses and government policy, although media campaigns and reports on human rights abuses in countries such as Syria can result in compassion fatigue and reduce people’s willingness to act. Despite their limitations, NGOs and the media inform, educate, and incite action, to effectively promote human rights.

items.samp: Universal suffrage refers to the right of all adults to vote in government elections so they can be involved in how they are governed. At the beginning of the 19th century only some men and no women could vote. Indigenous and racial minorities could not vote. During the 20th century the right to vote was extended to women and minorities, becoming a feature of democratic societies. Suffrage is now recognised in international law as a universal human right. For example, the General Assembly provides a forum for all member governments to raise human rights issues and concerns. The Assembly passes declarations condemning human rights abuses. items.samp: International responses are not very effective in enforcing human rights. Human rights laws are expected to be recognised and enforced by all sovereign nations. When this does not occur there will have been human rights abuses. An example is where nations such as Syria and China suppress freedom of political expression for minority groups. International calls to end this suppression have been ignored. In this way, international responses to human rights abuses can be restricted by the exercise of state sovereignty. An example of when international responses can effectively respond to human rights issues is when countries allow humanitarian intervention to allow aid workers to provide food, water, shelter and medical treatment for people displaced by war, as is the case in Syria. However, other countries would use state sovereignty to restrict access, for example Venezuela. When nations use their sovereignty to deny human rights such as labour rights, it is difficult for the United Nations to intervene. There are international bodies that can intervene to prosecute individuals such as the International Criminal Court, but this happens after the breaches have occurred. Only three prosecutions have been launched.

items.samp: State sovereignty is the ability of a nation state to make laws for its citizens without external interference. items.samp: A number of important human rights have been protected in Australia, although their enforceability varies. For instance, there are explicit rights contained in the Australian Constitution such as the right to vote in Commonwealth elections (s. 41). Similarly, statute law has contributed to the enforcement of human rights through the application of legislation such as the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth). Common law also reveals how Australia responds and enforces human rights, such as Dietrich v The Queen 1992. The High Court of Australia recognised the importance of a fair trial if the accused represents themselves or has an unqualified person representing them. This right, however, does not automatically allow the accused to acquire legal assistance if they did not meet the criteria for legal aid. The Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) was establised by the AHRC Act 1986 (Cth). However, this legislation, while establishing the statutory authority, may not lead to binding or enforceable judgements. Some Australian responses to the implementation of international law can also limit the enforcement of human rights. This can be seen with Australia’s interpretation of the Refugee Convention 1951 (UN) through the Migration Act 1958 (Cth).

items.samp: The Australian Constitution, established in 1901, provides a framework to reflect changing values and ethical standards through judicial interpretation, referendums and legislative reforms. The few explicit rights identified in the Constitution, such as the right to freedom of religion (Section 118) arguably leave gaps in protection. Further, the Constitution does not list what the Australian values are. Due to the complexity of the process, Constitutional reform is not often accomplished, for example the 1988 Rights and Freedoms referendum which aimed at enshrining civil rights failed. Conversely, the Constitution does allow the High Court to uphold implied rights and adapt to changing values. This occurred in the 1997 case, Lange v Australia Broadcasting Corporation, which upheld the existence of freedom of political communication. Additionally, the Constitution provides a framework to reflect changing values and ethical standards, however, has limitations due to the complexity of the reform progress.

items.samp: State sovereignty influences whether there is recognition, protection or enforcement of human rights, such as the right to be free from slavery. Positively, nation states can use their right to govern themselves without external interference to ratify and enact international laws that uphold human rights. For example, Australia ratified the 2000 Palermo Protocol by amending D. 270 of the Criminal Code 2005 (Cth) to criminalise slavery practices including servitude, forced labour and deceptive recruiting for labour or services. An example of enforcement is the case of R v Wei Tang 2008 HCA which was Australia’s first conviction under this amendment. On the other hand, sovereignty allows states to infringe upon the human rights of its citizens. For example, North Korea had the highest rate of people experiencing modern slavery in 2023. Due to state sovereignty, the international community is unable to interfere with global failures to uphold the right to be free from slavery.

items.samp: The media has a key role in influencing change in human rights because it provides a platform for raising awareness and advocating for action on issues of community concern. Whilst press freedom is a generally widely accepted right in democracies, it is not universally protected. For example, some countries impose media censorship on the reporting of issues. The media also has a significant responsibility to inform the public about human rights violations and inadequacies of existing laws eg treatment of asylum seekers. In this way, the media influences change in human rights. It acts as an important mechanism for ensuring accountability and transparency of law-making bodies and prompts the reform process eg Four Corners 2024 ‘Closure of Don Dale detention centre in the NT’.

items.sig: The prosecution must prove guilt: the accused never has to prove innocence.
items.lede: The prosecution must prove guilt: the accused never has to prove innocence. Reginald Woolmington, a 21-year-old farm labourer, was charged with murdering his 17-year-old wife Violet, who had left him three weeks earlier and was shot at her mother's house on 10 December 1934. He said the gun went off by accident while he was threatening to shoot himself. The first jury could not agree. At the second trial the judge told the jury that once the killing was proved the law presumed murder unless the prisoner satisfied them it was an accident. He was convicted and sentenced to death; the Court of Criminal Appeal applied the proviso and dismissed his appeal.

items.lede: The High Court held that a standard non-parole period is a guidepost, not a starting point: the judge still weighs every factor together. Derek Muldrock, 30, with an intellectual disability (a full-scale IQ of 62), pleaded guilty to sexual intercourse with a child under 10 — maximum 25 years, standard non-parole period (SNPP) 15 years. Chamanjot Singh, about 22, and Manpreet Kaur, 27, married in India in 2008 in a match that let one come to Australia on a study visa and the other as a dependent spouse. He offered a plea to manslaughter; the Crown refused it and tried him for murder. The jury acquitted of murder and convicted of manslaughter because the Crown could not disprove provocation.

items.lede: A self-represented appellant failed to overturn a declaration that three stop-start periods between 2019 and 2023 made a de facto relationship of at least two years. The AI-drafted grounds 'obscure the task of identification of error'. Appeal dismissed; no costs.

items.lede: A woman trapped in sexual servitude did not know she was a victim of modern slavery until she tried to leave and was told she owed $25,000 to get out. "Sarah" left a religious cult at 21, then a controlling relationship, and was isolated and in debt. A contact at the club where she was working introduced her to a man who said he could help her run her own business as a sex worker. He became controlling, demanded to know where she was, and influenced when and how she worked. She worked interstate and overseas, was pressured to provide services she had not consented to, and she and the other women were increasingly isolated and monitored. She escaped in 2020.

items.lede: He maintained his innocence for three years and pleaded guilty on the eve of his trial, having killed her within two weeks of release and in breach of an AVO. Mackenzie Anderson was killed in her Newcastle home in March 2022, not quite 22 years old. Tyrone Thompson, her former boyfriend, had served just over four months for assaulting and threatening her. He contacted her as soon as he was released, despite an AVO, and killed her less than two weeks after that release. On Tuesday 1 April 2025 he pleaded guilty to murder — after maintaining his innocence for three years, and on the eve of his trial in the NSW Supreme Court.

items.title: AFP youth radicalisation data
items.full: AFP data finds no single profile of a radicalised teenager (ABC, 27 October 2026)
items.sig: An AFP analysis of 55 radicalised boys aged 12 to 17 found all were drawn in at least partly online, three in five had mental health treatment, and no single family profile.
items.lede: An AFP analysis of 55 radicalised boys aged 12 to 17 found all were drawn in at least partly online, three in five had mental health treatment, and no single family profile. The AFP analysed 55 radicalised children, all boys aged 12 to 17. All were radicalised wholly or partly online (sometimes within days); about three in five had received mental health support; about a third had witnessed or experienced caregiver violence; over a quarter lacked a stable male role model, while some had secure family bonds. Jihadism was most common, but mixed or unclear ideologies are growing. Separately, 35 of 65 children targeted by counter-terrorism police since 2020 were charged.
