items.q: Which statement best defines a crime?
o: Conduct prohibited by the State and punishable by the criminal law
Any behaviour that most people consider immoral
A dispute between two parties settled by compensation
Any action that harms another person

e.why: A crime is a wrong against the community defined by law and punished by the State. Immoral or harmful conduct is not a crime unless the law says so, and civil disputes are about compensation between parties.

items.q: Sam punches Lee in a pub fight. Lee falls, hits his head and dies. To convict Sam of homicide, the prosecution must prove Sam's act was
o: a substantial and operating cause of Lee's death
the only cause of Lee's death
a possible cause of Lee's death
a cause that Sam foresaw in detail

e.why: Causation requires the act to be a substantial and operating cause of death (Royall v The Queen). It need not be the sole cause.

items.q: Which of the following is an offence against the person?

e.why: Assault harms or threatens a person directly. Larceny is a property offence, money laundering is an economic offence and offensive language is a public order offence.

items.q: Which of the following is a preliminary crime?

e.why: Preliminary crimes (attempt, conspiracy, incitement) punish steps taken towards an offence before it is completed.

items.q: Which of the following is a form of mens rea for murder in NSW?
o: Being present when a death occurs

e.why: Murder requires an intention to kill or cause grievous bodily harm, or reckless indifference to human life. Accidental death or mere presence does not meet that mental element.

items.q: A person who uses offensive language in a public place has most likely committed a

e.why: Offensive language is a minor public order offence dealt with summarily by a magistrate in the Local Court.

items.q: A rise in petrol drive-offs when fuel prices climb is best explained by which factor in crime?

e.why: Rising costs create financial pressure, which makes theft more attractive to some people, so economic factors are the best fit.

items.q: Community-led programs in Bourke that aim to address the causes of offending are best described as

e.why: Social prevention tackles underlying causes such as disadvantage and lack of opportunity. Situational prevention changes the environment to reduce opportunity.

items.q: Which person is a principal in the first degree?
o: The person who commits the criminal act
The person who plans the crime beforehand
The person who hides the offender afterwards
The person who keeps watch nearby

e.why: The principal in the first degree physically commits the offence. Planners are accessories before the fact, lookouts are principals in the second degree and those who help afterwards are accessories after the fact.

items.q: Which statement about summary offences is correct?
o: They are less serious and usually heard by a magistrate without a jury
They are always heard in the Supreme Court
They must be tried before a jury
They are heard only in the District Court

e.why: Summary offences are minor and dealt with in the Local Court by a magistrate alone. Indictable offences are more serious and may go to a jury trial in a higher court.

items.q: Under LEPRA, police may stop and search a person without a warrant if they have
o: reasonable grounds to suspect the person has a prohibited item
a neighbour's complaint with no detail
a belief the person is in a high crime suburb

e.why: Search powers without warrant need reasonable suspicion based on facts, not hunches or location alone. This protects individual liberty.

items.q: Under the Bail Act 2013 (NSW), the main question for a bail decision maker is whether there is
o: an unacceptable risk if the accused is released
a victim who objects to bail
a previous conviction of any kind

e.why: The Bail Act asks whether there is an unacceptable risk that the accused will fail to appear, commit a serious offence, endanger safety or interfere with witnesses. Guilt is not decided at bail.

items.q: When an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander person is taken into custody in NSW, police must notify
o: the Aboriginal Legal Service through the Custody Notification Service

e.why: The Custody Notification Service provides a legal check on the welfare of every Aboriginal person taken into custody, a response to deaths in custody.

items.q: Which Act regulates how police may take DNA samples and other forensic procedures from suspects in NSW?

e.why: The Crimes (Forensic Procedures) Act 2000 sets out when and how forensic procedures can be carried out, including consent and court orders.

items.q: What is true when a suspect is questioned by NSW police?
o: The suspect does not have to answer and must be cautioned before questioning
The suspect must answer if innocent
Silence counts as an admission of guilt
The suspect may stay silent only if a lawyer is present

e.why: The right to silence is a basic protection. Police must give a caution that the person does not have to say anything, and silence is not itself proof of guilt.

items.q: How can a member of the public assist the investigation of crime?
o: By reporting a suspected offence to police or Crime Stoppers
By deciding the charges that police lay

e.why: Reports from the public often start investigations. Charging, warrants and questioning are police and court functions.

items.q: Police can give a 'move on' direction to a person in a public place when their behaviour is
o: obstructing people or traffic or causing fear to others
a breach of the person's bail only

e.why: LEPRA lets police give reasonable directions where behaviour is obstructing others, harassing or intimidating, or involves supply of drugs. Appearance alone is not enough.

items.q: To detain a suspect for questioning beyond the initial investigation period, police need
o: a detention warrant from an authorised officer such as a magistrate

e.why: LEPRA caps the period police can detain a person for investigation. Extensions require a detention warrant from an authorised officer, giving judicial oversight.

items.q: Which is a purpose of attaching conditions to bail?
o: To reduce the risk the accused will reoffend or fail to appear while still allowing liberty
To punish the accused before trial
To prove the accused is guilty
To remove the right to silence

e.why: Bail conditions (reporting, curfews, surrender of passport) manage risk while respecting the presumption of innocence. They are not punishment.

items.q: The Farah Jama case (2009) demonstrates the importance of
o: reliable handling of forensic evidence such as DNA

e.why: Jama was wrongly convicted after DNA evidence was contaminated, showing why forensic evidence must be collected, stored and tested reliably.

items.q: Which court usually hears the most serious indictable offences such as murder in NSW?

e.why: Murder is tried in the Supreme Court. The Local Court deals with summary offences and committal hearings.

items.q: The 'golden thread' in Woolmington v DPP (1935) refers to the principle that
o: the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt

e.why: Woolmington confirmed the presumption of innocence: the burden of proof stays on the prosecution throughout.

items.q: In Dietrich v The Queen (1992) the High Court held that
o: an unrepresented accused facing a serious charge may have the trial stayed if it would be unfair
every accused has an absolute right to a free lawyer
legal aid must be given to all accused
a trial can proceed without a judge

e.why: The High Court recognised no absolute right to publicly funded counsel, but a trial may be stayed if lack of representation would make it unfair.

items.q: Which of the following is a role of the Public Defender?
o: To represent accused persons, especially in serious matters, often with legal aid
To prosecute the accused for the State

e.why: Public Defenders are barristers who represent accused persons, mostly in serious cases, supporting the right to legal representation.

items.q: Which statement about hearsay evidence is correct?
o: It is an out-of-court statement offered to prove its truth and is generally inadmissible, subject to exceptions
It only applies to expert witnesses
It is evidence given by the accused

e.why: The Evidence Act 1995 excludes hearsay because the maker cannot be cross-examined, but contains exceptions.

items.q: Evidence obtained illegally or improperly by police may be
o: excluded by the court unless admitting it is in the public interest

e.why: Section 138 of the Evidence Act requires a court to weigh the desirability of admitting evidence against the impropriety, so it is not automatically excluded.

items.q: For self-defence to succeed, the accused must have believed their conduct was necessary and it must have been
o: a reasonable response in the circumstances as the accused perceived them

e.why: Self-defence under the Crimes Act has a subjective belief element and an objective reasonableness test. If it succeeds, the accused is acquitted.

items.q: In NSW, jury panels are selected by the Sheriff

e.why: Random selection from the electoral roll aims for a representative jury. Both sides can then challenge some potential jurors.

items.q: Which reason might lead an accused to choose a judge-alone trial?
o: Concern that publicity or complex evidence may stop a jury being fair
To avoid a verdict being reasoned
To reduce the standard of proof

e.why: Judge-alone trials may be sought where publicity or complex evidence could prejudice a jury. The standard of proof does not change.

items.q: After an accused is acquitted, which statement is generally correct?
o: They cannot be tried again for the same offence, subject to limited statutory exceptions
They can be retried at the prosecution's choice
They must pay the court costs
They have a criminal record for the charge

e.why: Double jeopardy protects against repeated prosecution for the same offence. Statute allows retrials only in narrow cases, such as fresh and compelling evidence for very serious offences.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of sentencing under section 3A of the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999?
o: To pay compensation to the offender's family
To deter the offender and others

e.why: Section 3A lists punishment, deterrence, protection of the community, rehabilitation, accountability, denunciation and recognising harm to victims.

items.q: In Muldrock v The Queen (2011) the High Court held that the standard non-parole period is
o: a legislative guidepost, not the starting point for sentencing

e.why: Muldrock overturned the 'starting point' approach: judges consider all the circumstances and use the SNPP as a guidepost.

items.q: Bugmy v The Queen (2013) confirmed that
o: a deprived background can mitigate a sentence, but there is no special principle for Aboriginal offenders as a class
Aboriginal offenders must receive a lower sentence
deprivation reduces over time so it can be ignored

e.why: The High Court said courts must consider an offender's background of deprivation, but sentencing is based on individual circumstances.

items.q: An early guilty plea can reduce a sentence by up to about

e.why: Courts apply a discount of up to 25 per cent for an early guilty plea, recognising utility and remorse. The discount lowers with later pleas.

items.q: Circle sentencing in NSW is mainly designed to
o: involve Aboriginal Elders and the community in the sentencing process
allow victims to set the penalty

e.why: A magistrate leads a circle with Elders, the offender and victim support. It aims to increase community confidence and reduce reoffending.

items.q: Which sentence allows an offender to serve a prison sentence of up to two years in the community under supervision?

e.why: An Intensive Correction Order is a sentence of imprisonment served in the community with strict conditions as an alternative to full-time custody.

items.q: Which body can order continued detention or extended supervision of a high-risk offender after their sentence ends?

e.why: Under the Crimes (High Risk Offenders) Act 2006 the Supreme Court can order extended supervision or continued detention to protect the community.

items.q: The Victims Rights and Support Act 2013 provides victims of crime with
o: access to counselling and financial support
the power to choose the sentence
the right to appeal an acquittal
the right to cross-examine the accused

e.why: The Act sets out a Charter of Rights and the Victims Support Scheme, offering counselling and financial assistance but not control over prosecution or sentence.

items.q: The DPP may appeal a sentence on the ground that it is
o: too lenient only because the victim disagrees

e.why: Crown sentence appeals are limited to sentences that are manifestly inadequate, which respects the offender's interest in finality.

items.q: Mandatory minimum sentences such as those in the one-punch laws reduce

e.why: Mandatory sentences limit the judge's ability to weigh individual circumstances, which is why they are controversial.

items.q: A key aim of the Young Offenders Act 1997 is to
o: divert young offenders from court where appropriate
impose longer sentences on young people
remove their right to a lawyer

e.why: The Act provides alternatives to formal prosecution that hold the young person accountable while encouraging rehabilitation.

items.q: The presumption of doli incapax in NSW applies to children aged

e.why: Children under 10 cannot be criminally responsible. For 10 to 13, the prosecution must rebut the presumption of doli incapax.

items.q: In RP v The Queen (2016) the High Court emphasised that to rebut doli incapax the prosecution must
o: prove the child knew the act was seriously wrong, with evidence beyond the act itself
rely only on the seriousness of the offence

e.why: RP stresses that the presumption protects children and must be rebutted by evidence of the child's understanding of seriously wrong conduct.

items.q: Under the Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987, the media is generally prohibited from
o: publishing the name of a child involved in criminal proceedings

e.why: Name suppression protects young people's privacy and rehabilitation prospects.

items.q: Which is a feature of the Children's Court?
o: Proceedings are closed to the public and heard by a magistrate without a jury
Cases are heard by a jury
Hearings are always open to the media

e.why: The Children's Court is a specialised, closed court focused on rehabilitation, using a magistrate rather than a jury.

items.q: The Youth Koori Court differs from an ordinary Children's Court because it
o: involves Elders and creates an action plan with the young person

e.why: It is a culturally appropriate sentencing court where Elders and support people help a young Aboriginal person address the causes of offending.

items.q: A youth justice conference brings together
o: the young person, the victim, a convenor and support people

e.why: Conferences are a restorative process in which participants agree on an outcome plan to repair harm.

items.q: Which is a reason for treating young offenders differently from adults?
o: They are still maturing and have greater potential for rehabilitation
They are less likely to reoffend

e.why: Developmental differences and rehabilitation prospects justify specialised courts, diversion and sentencing principles.

items.q: Queensland's 'adult crime, adult time' laws are an example of
o: a punitive approach to young offenders that moves away from rehabilitation

e.why: These laws increase penalties for serious youth offending and have been criticised for reducing the emphasis on rehabilitation.

items.q: A 16-year-old is charged with armed robbery. The matter will most likely be heard in the

e.why: Most offences by children are dealt with in the Children's Court. Only the most serious indictable offences are heard in higher courts.

items.q: Which statement about the minimum age of criminal responsibility in NSW is correct?
o: Children under 10 cannot be held criminally responsible

e.why: The minimum age is 10. Between 10 and 13, doli incapax requires proof that the child understood the act was seriously wrong.

items.q: Under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW), which order lists responses from least to most formal?
o: Warning, caution, youth justice conference, Children's Court

e.why: The Act provides a hierarchy of diversion: warnings, cautions and conferences before court, for eligible offences.

items.q: The ICC has jurisdiction over which crimes?
o: Genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression

e.why: The Rome Statute gives the ICC jurisdiction over four core crimes of international concern.

items.q: The principle of complementarity means the ICC acts only when
o: national courts are unwilling or unable to genuinely prosecute
a state asks for a trial

e.why: The ICC is a court of last resort. States have the primary responsibility to investigate and prosecute.

items.q: A major limitation on the ICC when seeking to enforce the Putin warrant is that it
o: has no police force and relies on states to arrest suspects

e.why: The ICC relies on state cooperation. Russia is not a party to the Rome Statute and does not recognise the warrant.

items.q: In South Africa v Israel the International Court of Justice resolves

e.why: The ICJ hears disputes between states. The ICC tries individuals.

items.q: The UN Convention against Transnational Organised Crime (UNTOC) encourages states to
o: cooperate and criminalise participation in organised crime groups

e.why: UNTOC provides a framework for international cooperation, including mutual legal assistance and extradition.

items.q: Extradition from Australia to another country is regulated by

e.why: The Commonwealth Act sets out the process for requests, including judicial and ministerial decisions.

items.q: Which Australian laws address human trafficking and slavery offences?
o: Criminal Code (Cth) and the Modern Slavery Act

e.why: Commonwealth laws criminalise trafficking and slavery and require large entities to report on modern slavery risks.

items.q: The ICTY was
o: an ad hoc tribunal set up by the UN Security Council to prosecute crimes in the former Yugoslavia

e.why: The ICTY (1993 to 2017) was a temporary tribunal and a forerunner to the permanent ICC.

items.q: A key difficulty in investigating transnational crime is that
o: laws and jurisdiction differ between countries and evidence may be held overseas

e.why: Differences in laws, sovereignty and the location of evidence make cooperation essential.

items.q: Australia's use of targeted cyber sanctions after the Medibank hack is an example of
o: a non-judicial response to transnational crime

e.why: Sanctions impose financial and travel restrictions on individuals without a trial, supplementing judicial responses.

items.q: Which term describes the mental element of a crime?

e.why: Mens rea is the guilty mind (intention, recklessness or criminal negligence). Actus reus is the physical act.

items.q: Why is speeding classed as a strict liability offence?
o: The prosecution must prove the driver intended to speed
It can only be heard in the District Court
The prosecution only needs to prove the act, not a guilty mind
No penalty can be imposed for it

e.why: Strict liability offences need proof of the actus reus only. An honest and reasonable mistake of fact can still be raised.

items.lead: Sam punches Lee. Lee falls, hits his head and later dies in hospital from the head injury.
items.q: Which element must the prosecution prove to link Sam's punch to Lee's death?

e.why: Causation requires an unbroken link between the accused's act and the harm.

items.q: Which statement about summary offences in NSW is correct?
o: They are heard by a judge and jury in the District Court
They are less serious offences heard by a magistrate in the Local Court
They always begin with a committal hearing
They can only be prosecuted by the Director of Public Prosecutions

e.why: Summary offences are finalised in the Local Court by a magistrate sitting alone, usually with a police prosecutor.

items.lead: Jo keeps watch at the door while Kim robs a shop.
items.q: What is Jo's role in the crime?

e.why: A principal in the second degree is present and assists while the crime is committed. Kim, who commits the act, is the principal in the first degree.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of situational crime prevention?
o: A parenting program for young families
Extra funding for school attendance officers
Better street lighting and CCTV at a train station

e.why: Situational prevention makes a crime harder or riskier to commit in a place. The other options are social prevention, which targets the causes of offending.

items.q: Which Act sets out most police powers in NSW, including search, arrest and detention?

e.why: The Act, known as LEPRA, brought police powers together in one statute and sets safeguards on their use.

items.q: Under the Bail Act 2013 (NSW), what must a bail authority consider for every accused person?
o: Whether the accused is likely to be found guilty
Whether there is an unacceptable risk that cannot be managed by conditions
Whether the victim agrees to bail
Whether the accused can afford a lawyer

e.why: The unacceptable risk test asks about failing to appear, committing a serious offence, endangering safety and interfering with witnesses or evidence.

items.q: Which statement best describes the right to silence for a suspect questioned by police in NSW?
o: A suspect must answer every question once cautioned
A suspect generally need not answer questions, other than giving details such as name and address when required by law
The right applies only to people under 18
The right is lost once a person is arrested

e.why: Police must caution a suspect that they do not have to say or do anything. Some laws require identity details to be given.

items.q: Which court hears most trials for serious indictable offences such as armed robbery in NSW?

e.why: The District Court hears most indictable offences. The Supreme Court hears the most serious, such as murder.

items.q: Which is a feature of the adversary system?
o: The judge leads the investigation and questions witnesses
Two opposing sides present their cases before an impartial decision-maker
The accused must prove their innocence
Evidence is collected by the court itself

e.why: In the adversary system the parties run their own cases and the judge or magistrate is an impartial umpire.

items.q: What is charge negotiation?
o: The magistrate reducing a sentence after hearing a victim impact statement
An agreement in which the accused pleads guilty in return for a lesser or fewer charges
The jury agreeing on a majority verdict
Police deciding whether to issue a caution

e.why: Charge negotiation takes place between the prosecution and the defence before trial. It saves court time but can be seen as lenient.

items.q: What is the standard of proof in a criminal trial?

e.why: The prosecution carries the burden and must prove the offence beyond reasonable doubt.

items.q: Which of the following is a partial defence to murder in NSW?
o: Substantial impairment because of mental health impairment or cognitive impairment

e.why: A partial defence reduces murder to manslaughter. Self-defence, duress and necessity are complete defences that lead to an acquittal.

items.q: How many jurors usually sit on a criminal trial in NSW, and what verdict can be accepted?
o: Six jurors; the verdict must be unanimous
Twelve jurors; a majority verdict of 11 to 1 may be accepted after long deliberation
Twelve jurors; a simple majority of 7 to 5 is enough
Four jurors; the verdict must be unanimous

e.why: The Jury Act 1977 (NSW) allows a majority verdict of 11 to 1 when a unanimous verdict cannot be reached after reasonable time.

items.q: A judge says the sentence must "send a message to others who might think of committing this offence". Which purpose of punishment is this?

e.why: General deterrence aims to discourage the wider community. Specific deterrence aims at the offender.

items.q: Which of the following is a mitigating factor in sentencing?
o: The offence was committed in company
The offender showed remorse and pleaded guilty early

e.why: Mitigating factors can reduce a sentence. The other options are aggravating factors under s 21A of the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW).

items.q: Which penalty allows an offender to serve a sentence of imprisonment in the community under strict supervision?

e.why: An intensive correction order is a custodial sentence served in the community, with conditions such as home detention, curfews or community service.

items.q: What is parole?
o: A sentence served entirely in the community
The conditional release of a prisoner to serve the rest of the sentence in the community under supervision
A reduction in sentence for a guilty plea
An order made after a sentence has ended

e.why: Parole helps reintegration under supervision. Breaching conditions can return the offender to custody.

items.q: What does doli incapax mean for a child aged 10 to under 14 in NSW?
o: The child can never be charged with an offence
The child is presumed incapable of criminal intent unless the prosecution proves the child knew the act was seriously wrong
The child must be tried as an adult
The child's parents are criminally responsible

e.why: The presumption can be rebutted. RP v The Queen (2016) confirmed the prosecution must prove the child knew the conduct was seriously wrong in a moral sense.

items.q: Which options does the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) provide as alternatives to court?
o: Warnings, cautions and youth justice conferences

e.why: The Act diverts young people from court for less serious offences, in increasing order of seriousness.

items.q: Which of the following is a transnational crime rather than a crime against the international community?

e.why: Transnational crimes cross borders and are prosecuted under domestic law. Genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity can be tried by the International Criminal Court.

items.q: What is a limitation of the International Criminal Court?
o: It can only hear civil disputes between countries
It has no police force and relies on states to arrest and surrender suspects
It can only try people under 18
Its decisions must be approved by the High Court of Australia

e.why: The Court depends on state cooperation, and several powerful states are not parties to the Rome Statute.

items.q: What is circle sentencing?
o: A sentencing hearing held by three judges
An alternative sentencing court for adult Aboriginal offenders that involves Elders and community members
A program in which prisoners move between prisons
A type of youth justice conference for first offenders

e.why: The magistrate sits with Elders, the offender, and often the victim, to discuss the offence and an appropriate sentence.

items.q: Distinguish between a strict liability offence and an offence that requires mens rea. Use an example of each.
pts: Mens rea offences need proof of a guilty mind as well as the act, for example murder or larceny (1)
Strict liability offences need proof of the act only, for example speeding (1)
Shows the difference clearly, such as what the prosecution must prove (1)

items.q: Explain how the Bail Act 2013 (NSW) tries to balance the rights of the accused with the safety of the community.
pts: Bail lets an accused stay in the community until trial, which respects the presumption of innocence (1)
The unacceptable risk test protects the community, victims and witnesses (1)
Show cause offences place the onus on the accused for serious charges (1)
Conditions such as reporting or curfews can manage risk without remand (1)

items.q: Explain why access to legal representation is important in a criminal trial. Refer to one case.
pts: The adversary system assumes both sides are equally able to present a case (1)
An unrepresented accused faces a trained prosecutor and complex rules of evidence (1)
Dietrich v The Queen (1992): a trial for a serious offence may be stayed if the accused cannot get representation through no fault of their own (1)
Legal Aid NSW applies a means test, a merit test and a jurisdiction test, so some people miss out (1)

items.q: Outline the role of the victim in sentencing.
pts: A victim may give a victim impact statement about the harm suffered (1)
It is read or given to the court after conviction and before sentence (1)
The court may take it into account, but the sentence is still the court's decision (1)

items.q: Describe TWO ways the Children's Court operates differently from an adult court.
pts: It is a closed court and the child's name cannot generally be published (2 for a described feature)
Proceedings are less formal, and the magistrate must make sure the child understands (2 for a second described feature)
items.ans: Other acceptable features: a specialist magistrate sits without a jury; rehabilitation is given priority; penalties come from the Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW).

items.q: Assess the effectiveness of ONE domestic or international measure in dealing with international crime.
pts: Names a measure, such as the International Criminal Court, extradition treaties or the Australian Federal Police working with Interpol (1)
Explains how it works (1)
Gives at least one strength with evidence (1)
Gives at least one limit, such as state sovereignty, cost or delay (1)
Makes a judgement about its effectiveness (1)

items.lead: Police stop Dani, aged 22, outside a shopping centre after a staff member reports that someone matching her description put a phone in her bag without paying. An officer searches her bag without a warrant, finds an unopened phone and arrests her. At the station she is questioned for two hours without being told she does not have to answer.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Identify the power police used to search Dani's bag and what they needed before using it.
pts: A search without a warrant under the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW) (1)
Police must suspect on reasonable grounds that she has something stolen (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain whether police acted lawfully at the station. Refer to the scenario.
pts: Police must caution a suspect that they do not have to say or do anything (1)
Dani was not cautioned, so this safeguard was breached (1)
She should also be told of her right to contact a lawyer or support person, and the detention time limits apply (1)
A court has a discretion to exclude evidence that was improperly obtained (1)

items.lead: Marco is walking home when a stranger grabs him from behind and threatens him with a broken bottle. Marco pushes the man hard. The man falls, strikes his head on the kerb and is seriously injured. Marco is charged with recklessly causing grievous bodily harm.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Identify the defence Marco is most likely to raise.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain how a court would decide whether the defence succeeds. Refer to the scenario.
pts: Marco must have believed his conduct was necessary to defend himself (1)
His response must be reasonable in the circumstances as he perceived them (1)
A threat with a broken bottle supports both parts of the test (1)
Once the defence is raised, the prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt; if it cannot, Marco is acquitted (1)

items.lead: Tayla, aged 12, is caught spraying paint on a bus shelter. She has never been in trouble with police before. Police take her to the station and want to ask her questions. Her mother is at work and cannot be reached.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Outline how doli incapax applies to Tayla.
pts: She is aged 10 to under 14, so she is presumed incapable of criminal intent (1)
The prosecution would need to prove she knew the act was seriously wrong (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain why police should not interview Tayla alone.
pts: A child should have a responsible adult present when questioned (1)
A statement made without one may not be admitted as evidence (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Recommend the most suitable response under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW). Give reasons.
pts: A warning or a caution (1)
The offence is minor, non-violent and her first (1)
Diversion avoids a court record and reduces the risk of reoffending (1)

items.lead: Ravi, aged 34, pleads guilty at the first opportunity to breaking into a house at night while the family was asleep. He stole jewellery worth $4,000. He has two earlier convictions for similar offences. He has since begun treatment for drug addiction and has written a letter of apology to the family.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Identify ONE aggravating factor and ONE mitigating factor in the scenario.
pts: Aggravating: prior convictions, or the offence took place in a home at night with the occupants present (1)
Mitigating: early guilty plea, remorse or steps towards rehabilitation (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain which purposes of punishment a court might give most weight to when sentencing Ravi.
pts: Names relevant purposes, such as specific deterrence, protection of the community and rehabilitation (1)
Links deterrence or protection to his record (1)
Links rehabilitation to his treatment (1)
Shows the court must balance competing purposes (1)

items.q: Evaluate the role of discretion in achieving justice in the criminal justice system.
pts: Defines discretion and names who uses it: police, prosecutors, magistrates and judges, juries
Police discretion: warnings and cautions under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW); decisions to arrest and charge under the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW)
Prosecutorial discretion: charge negotiation and the prosecution guidelines
Judicial discretion in sentencing: s 21A factors, guideline judgments, and limits such as standard non-parole periods and mandatory sentences
Weighs individualised justice against inconsistency and possible bias, using cases, media and reports
Makes a sustained judgement
plan: Police: flexibility for minor and young offenders, but uneven use
Prosecution and pre-trial: efficiency against transparency
Judgement: discretion is necessary but needs guidelines and review

items.q: To what extent does the criminal justice system deal effectively with young offenders?
pts: Age of criminal responsibility and doli incapax (RP v The Queen 2016), and the debate about raising the age
Rights when questioned and arrested
Children's Court procedures and the focus on rehabilitation
Diversion under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) and the Youth Koori Court
Penalties, detention and reoffending, with statistics from a named source
Over-representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people
A judgement that addresses "to what extent"
plan: Different treatment is justified: age and capacity
Diversion works for most young people

items.q: Assess how effectively the criminal trial and sentencing processes balance the rights of victims, offenders and society.
pts: Rights of the accused: presumption of innocence, legal representation (Dietrich v The Queen 1992), rules of evidence, appeals
Rights of victims: the Charter of Victims Rights, victim impact statements, support services
Society: open justice, juries, the purposes of punishment
Tensions: charge negotiation, bail, sentencing discounts, mandatory sentences
A judgement on the balance, with a range of evidence
plan: Victims: growing recognition but a limited role

items.q: Assess the effectiveness of bail laws in balancing the rights of the accused and the protection of the community.
pts: A judgement, for example that the law now favours community protection
Evidence: Bail Act 2013 (NSW), the show cause requirement and the unacceptable risk test
Analysis against a criterion, such as protection of individual rights or meeting society's needs
Counterpoint: the growing remand population and the presumption of innocence
A link back to the question

items.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of alternative methods of sentencing in achieving justice.
pts: A judgement about circle sentencing or restorative justice
Evidence: the program, who takes part and what research from a named source found
Analysis against a criterion, such as responsiveness or reducing reoffending
Counterpoint: limited places, eligibility rules or mixed results
A link back to the question

items.title: An indictable offence, from arrest to sentence
items.blurb: An adult is accused of a serious indictable offence in NSW and pleads not guilty.
steps: Police arrest and charge the suspect
A bail decision is made
The charge is first mentioned in the Local Court
The matter is committed to the District Court for trial
A jury is empanelled
The prosecution and the defence present their evidence
The jury gives its verdict
The judge sentences the offender
items.closing: Every indictable matter starts in the Local Court. Only the higher court can hold the trial.

items.title: The order of a criminal trial
steps: The prosecution makes its opening address
Prosecution witnesses give evidence in chief
The defence cross-examines prosecution witnesses
The defence presents its case
Both sides give closing addresses
The judge sums up and directs the jury on the law
The jury retires to consider its verdict
items.closing: The prosecution goes first because it carries the burden of proof.

items.title: Responses to a young offender, from least to most serious
steps: Warning
Caution
Youth justice conference
Children's Court hearing
Control order (detention)
items.closing: The Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) requires the least restrictive suitable response.

items.title: How a crisis can change bail law
items.trigger: A person on bail commits a serious violent offence that is widely reported.

steps.v: The media report the case and question the bail decision
steps.why: Media coverage shapes public opinion about the law.

steps.v: The community and victims' groups call for tougher laws
steps.why: Public pressure reaches members of parliament.

steps.v: The government announces a review or a bill
steps.why: Parliament responds to keep public confidence.

steps.v: More accused people are refused bail
steps.why: The test is harder to meet.
More people who have not been convicted are held in custody.

items.q: Sort each feature under the correct type of offence.

rows.t: Usually prosecuted by a police prosecutor
Tried by a judge and jury
Heard in the District Court or the Supreme Court
Prosecuted by the Director of Public Prosecutions

items.q: Sort each defence under the correct heading.

rows.t: Mental health impairment or cognitive impairment

items.q: Match each sentencing remark to the purpose of punishment it shows.

rows.t: "Others must see that this conduct brings a heavy penalty."
"You will think twice before doing this again."
"The sentence must reflect the harm done to the victim."
"You must complete a drug treatment program."
"Counselling will address the causes of your offending."
"The community needs to be protected from you."
"Your licence is disqualified for five years."

items.q: Complete the table to compare how a child and an adult are treated by the criminal justice system in NSW.

cells.t: All purposes are weighed, including deterrence and retribution
Warnings, cautions and conferences under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW)
Limited, for example some cautions and diversion programs
Detention in a youth justice centre

items.q: Complete the table to compare the adversary system with the inquisitorial system.

cells.t: Leads the inquiry and questions witnesses
Australia and other common law countries
Each side can test the other's case
Less depends on the skill of the lawyers
Depends on equal resources and representation
The judge may be less impartial

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline the role of the jury in a criminal trial."
items.text: In a criminal trial in the District Court, a jury of [[six => twelve]] people decides whether the accused is guilty. The jury decides questions of [[law => fact]], while the judge decides questions of law. The [[defence => prosecution]] must prove its case [[on the balance of probabilities => beyond reasonable doubt]]. If the jury finds the accused guilty, the [[jury => judge]] decides the sentence.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Describe the rights of a suspect who has been arrested in NSW."
items.text: Police powers of arrest are set out in the [[Bail Act 2013 => Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002]] (NSW). Before questioning, police must [[interview => caution]] the suspect, who has a right to silence. A suspect can usually be detained for investigation for up to [[twenty-four => six]] hours before being charged or released, and a longer period needs a [[search warrant => detention warrant]]. A suspect is entitled to contact a lawyer.

items.title: Prison numbers and reoffending
items.lede: A state report finds that the number of adults in prison has grown faster than the population over ten years. About four in ten adults released from prison return to custody within two years. The report says short prison sentences give little time for treatment programs, while supervised orders served in the community cost far less per day and have lower reoffending rates for comparable offenders.
items.by: Constructed source for practice. The figures are invented.

qs.q: Outline ONE finding of the report.
pts: States a finding accurately (1)
Adds detail from the source (1)

qs.q: Explain what the source suggests about how well imprisonment achieves the purposes of punishment.
pts: Imprisonment achieves incapacitation and retribution (1)
A high return-to-custody rate suggests weak specific deterrence (1)
Short sentences limit rehabilitation (1)
Community-based orders may achieve rehabilitation at lower cost (1)

qs.q: Assess the effectiveness of ONE penalty other than imprisonment.
pts: Names a penalty, such as an intensive correction order or a community correction order (1)
Explains how it works under the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW) (1)
Gives a strength with evidence (1)
Gives a limit (1)
Makes a judgement (1)

items.q: Which level of government makes laws about marriage and divorce in Australia?
o: The states, under their residual powers

e.why: The Constitution gives the Commonwealth power over marriage and divorce. The states keep areas such as adoption and child protection.

items.q: What is the marriageable age in Australia?
o: 18, or 16 to 17 with a court order in exceptional circumstances

e.why: The Marriage Act 1961 (Cth) sets 18. A person aged 16 or 17 needs a court order and parental consent to marry someone who is 18 or over.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a requirement of a valid marriage in Australia?
o: A notice of intended marriage is given at least one month before the wedding
The ceremony is held in a religious building

e.why: A marriage can be held anywhere by an authorised celebrant. Consent, notice and witnesses are required.

items.q: What must be shown to obtain a divorce in Australia?
o: That one spouse was at fault
That the marriage has broken down irretrievably, shown by 12 months of separation
That both spouses agree to the divorce
That the couple have no children

e.why: The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) introduced no-fault divorce. Neither fault nor agreement is needed.

items.q: What is the paramount consideration when a court makes a parenting order?
o: The best interests of the child

e.why: The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) makes the child's best interests paramount. There is no rule that time must be equal.

items.q: What did the Family Law Amendment Act 2023 (Cth) change about parenting orders?
o: It removed the best interests test
It removed the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility
It moved parenting cases to the Local Court

e.why: From May 2024 the presumption introduced in 2006 no longer applies, and the list of best interests factors was simplified with a stronger focus on safety.

items.q: How does a court divide property after a marriage ends?
o: Each person keeps what is in their name
The court makes an order that is just and equitable after weighing contributions and future needs
The person who earned more receives everything

e.why: The court counts financial and non-financial contributions, including homemaking and parenting, and each person's future needs.

items.q: Which statement about an apprehended domestic violence order in NSW is correct?
o: It is a civil order, but breaching it is a criminal offence
It can only be applied for by the victim

e.why: The order is made under the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW). Police often apply on the victim's behalf.

items.q: Which court hears most parenting and property disputes after separation?
o: The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia
The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal

e.why: The court was formed in 2021. The Children's Court hears care and protection matters under NSW law.

items.q: Which change gave same-sex couples the right to marry in Australia?
o: An amendment to the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth) in December 2017

e.why: Parliament changed the definition of marriage to "the union of 2 people" after the postal survey. It was a survey, not a referendum.

items.q: Which statement about surrogacy in NSW is correct?
o: Commercial surrogacy is legal if it is arranged overseas
The intended parents are the legal parents from birth
Surrogacy agreements are enforced by the courts

e.why: The Surrogacy Act 2010 (NSW) bans commercial surrogacy, including overseas arrangements by NSW residents. Parentage is transferred by a court order.

items.q: Which Act allows a child at risk of significant harm to be removed from the family home in NSW?
o: Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998 (NSW)

e.why: The Act governs reports, investigations and care orders made by the Children's Court.

items.q: Explain how the law recognises de facto relationships.
pts: A de facto couple live together on a genuine domestic basis (1)
Courts look at factors such as how long they have lived together and shared finances (1)
Since 2009 the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) has covered property and maintenance for most de facto couples (1)
Children are treated the same whether or not their parents are married (1)

items.q: Explain why the law encourages families to resolve disputes without going to court.
pts: Family dispute resolution is usually required before applying for a parenting order (1)
It is cheaper and faster than a hearing (1)
Agreements parents make themselves are more likely to last (1)
It reduces conflict that harms children (1)
A limit: it is not suitable where there is family violence or an imbalance of power (1)

items.lead: Priya and Tom married eight years ago and have a daughter, Mia, aged 6. They separated ten months ago but still live in the same house because neither can afford to move out. Tom wants a divorce now. Priya wants Mia to live mainly with her.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Explain whether Tom can apply for a divorce now.
pts: The ground is irretrievable breakdown, shown by 12 months of separation (1)
Only ten months have passed, so he must wait (1)
Separation under one roof can count, but it must be proved (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain how a decision about Mia's living arrangements would be made if Priya and Tom cannot agree.
pts: They must usually try family dispute resolution first (1)
A court can then make a parenting order (1)
Mia's best interests are the paramount consideration (1)
The court considers her safety, her views and her need for a relationship with both parents where that is safe (1)

items.lead: Over two years, Jordan's partner has checked Jordan's phone every day, controlled all the money, and stopped Jordan from seeing friends. Last week the partner threatened to hurt Jordan if Jordan left. Jordan lives in NSW and is frightened.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Identify TWO legal protections available to Jordan.
pts: An apprehended domestic violence order (1)
Criminal charges, such as for intimidation or coercive control (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Assess how effective these protections are likely to be.
pts: An order sets clear conditions and police can apply for it (1)
A breach is a criminal offence (1)
Limits: orders are sometimes breached and victims may fear reporting (1)
A judgement, with reference to support services or recent reform (1)

items.lead: Elena and Chris were married for 15 years. Chris worked full time and paid the mortgage. Elena left paid work to care for their three children and now earns much less than Chris. The house is in Chris's name only. They have separated and cannot agree on how to divide their property.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Outline TWO types of contribution a court would consider.
pts: Financial contributions, such as income and mortgage payments (1)
Non-financial contributions, such as homemaking and caring for children (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain why Elena could receive a share of the house even though it is in Chris's name.
pts: The court looks at all the property of both people, whoever holds title (1)
Her contributions as homemaker and parent are recognised (1)
Future needs matter: her lower earning capacity and care of the children (1)
The order must be just and equitable in all the circumstances (1)

items.q: To what extent has family law responded to changing community values?
pts: The changing concept of family
No-fault divorce under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth)
Recognition of de facto and same-sex relationships, including the 2017 change to the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth)
Parental responsibility: the 2006 and 2023 reforms
Surrogacy and birth technologies
Domestic violence: recognition of coercive control
Areas where the law lags, with media and reports as evidence
A sustained judgement on extent
plan: Relationships: the law caught up slowly, then decisively
Children: from parents' rights to children's safety
New technology: the law trails practice
Violence: values changed first, the law followed

items.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of legal and non-legal responses in protecting family members from harm.
pts: Domestic violence: apprehended domestic violence orders, police powers, the coercive control offence
Children: mandatory reporting, the Children's Court, out-of-home care
Family Law Act 1975 (Cth): safety in parenting decisions
Non-legal responses: refuges, helplines, non-government organisations and the media
Limits: under-reporting, breaches, resources, remote communities
A judgement using criteria such as enforceability, accessibility and protection of rights

items.q: Assess the effectiveness of law reform in protecting the best interests of children after separation.
pts: A judgement about the 2023 reforms
Evidence: Family Law Amendment Act 2023 (Cth) and what it removed
Analysis against protection of rights or responsiveness
Counterpoint: cost and delay in the courts remain
A link back to the question

items.title: Resolving a parenting dispute after separation
steps: The parents separate
The parents try to agree between themselves, perhaps in a parenting plan
The parents attend family dispute resolution
A certificate is issued if no agreement is reached
One parent applies to the court for a parenting order
The court considers the best interests of the child
The court makes a parenting order
items.closing: Court is the last step. Cases involving family violence or urgency can skip dispute resolution.

items.q: Sort each area of family law under the level of government mainly responsible for it.
Complete the table to compare marriage with a de facto relationship.

cells.t: A ceremony that meets the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth)
The couple live together on a genuine domestic basis
Evidence such as shared finances, a shared home and how others see the couple
Separation; no court order is needed
Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), if the relationship meets the tests
Treated the same under the law
Treated the same under the law

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline the law on divorce in Australia."
items.text: Divorce is governed by the [[Marriage Act 1961 => Family Law Act 1975]] (Cth). The only ground is that the marriage has broken down irretrievably, shown by [[six => 12]] months of separation. The court [[must => does not]] consider who was at fault. If there are children under 18, the court must be satisfied that [[the parents have equal time => proper arrangements have been made for their care]].

items.q: Which word describes human rights as belonging to all people everywhere?

e.why: Universal means the rights apply to everyone. Inalienable means they cannot be taken away.

items.q: Why is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights described as soft law?
o: It applies only to developed countries
It is a declaration that is not legally binding on states
It was replaced by the United Nations Charter
It can be enforced by the International Criminal Court

e.why: A declaration states principles. It has great moral force and inspired binding treaties such as the two 1966 covenants.

items.q: Which of the following is a collective right?
o: The right to a fair trial
The right to freedom of religion

e.why: Self-determination belongs to a people as a group. The other options are individual civil and political rights.

items.q: How can state sovereignty limit the protection of human rights?
o: States must obey every resolution of the General Assembly
A state can refuse to ratify a treaty or to let outside bodies review its conduct
Sovereign states cannot make their own laws
Sovereignty lets individuals sue their government in any court

e.why: International law depends largely on consent. A state can decline to sign, ratify or comply.

items.q: Which United Nations body can authorise binding measures such as sanctions?

e.why: Security Council resolutions can bind member states, but any of the five permanent members can veto them.

items.q: Which statement about the International Court of Justice is correct?
o: It tries individuals for war crimes
It hears disputes between states that accept its jurisdiction
It hears complaints from individuals against their own government
It is part of the Australian court hierarchy

e.why: Only states can be parties before the Court. Individuals are tried by the International Criminal Court.

items.q: Australia has a dualist system. What does this mean for a human rights treaty that Australia has ratified?
o: It becomes part of Australian law at once
It has no effect in domestic law until parliament passes legislation to give it effect
It applies only in the territories

e.why: Parliament must enact a treaty, as it did in part with the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth).

items.q: Which right is expressly protected by the Australian Constitution?

e.why: Section 116 stops the Commonwealth making laws to establish a religion or prohibit its free exercise. Freedom of political communication is implied, not express.

items.q: Which is an argument against a national Charter of Rights for Australia?
o: It would educate people about their rights
It would bring Australia into line with other democracies
It could shift power from elected parliaments to unelected judges

e.why: Opponents say rights are already protected by parliament, the common law and the Constitution, and that a charter could give judges too much power.

items.q: Which of the following is a non-government organisation that promotes human rights?
o: The United Nations Human Rights Council

e.why: Amnesty International is independent of government. It investigates and reports on abuses and campaigns for change.

items.q: Which case is an example of the High Court finding an implied freedom in the Constitution?

e.why: The Court held that the system of representative government in the Constitution implies a freedom of political communication.

items.q: Outline how recognition of ONE human right has developed over time.
pts: Names a right, such as freedom from slavery, universal suffrage or universal education (1)
Describes an early stage, such as a campaign or a national law (1)
Describes later international recognition, such as an article of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1)

items.q: Explain the role of the United Nations in promoting and enforcing human rights.
pts: The General Assembly adopts declarations and treaties (1)
The Human Rights Council reviews each state's record (1)
The Security Council can impose sanctions or authorise intervention (1)
Treaty committees monitor compliance with reports (1)
A limit, such as the veto or reliance on state consent (1)

items.q: Compare the protection of human rights by statute law and by common law in Australia.
pts: Statute: parliament enacts specific protections, such as the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) (1)
Statute can be changed or repealed by a later parliament (1)
Common law: judges recognise rights case by case, such as the right to a fair trial in Dietrich v The Queen (1992) (1)
Common law can be overridden by clear legislation (1)
A similarity (1)
A difference stated clearly (1)

items.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of legal responses to ONE contemporary human rights issue.
pts: Names and outlines the issue (1)
International legal responses, with a named instrument (1 to 2)
Domestic legal responses, with named legislation or a case (1 to 2)
Limits, such as sovereignty or enforcement (1)
A reasoned judgement (1)

items.lead: Amira applies for a job as a sales assistant. The manager tells her she interviewed well but that customers "would not be comfortable" with her headscarf, and gives the job to someone else. Amira wants to know what she can do.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Identify the type of law that protects Amira and ONE body she could complain to.
pts: Anti-discrimination legislation, such as the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) or the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) (1)
The Australian Human Rights Commission or Anti-Discrimination NSW (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain how her complaint would be dealt with and what might limit the outcome.
pts: The body investigates and tries to conciliate the complaint (1)
If conciliation fails she can take the matter to a court or tribunal (1)
Remedies can include an apology or compensation (1)
Limits include cost, time, proof and gaps in the grounds each Act covers (1)

items.q: To what extent does state sovereignty limit the protection of human rights?
pts: A judgement about extent
Evidence: a named treaty or body and a named example of a state refusing to comply
Analysis against enforceability
Counterpoint: sovereignty is also how rights become domestic law

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline how human rights are formally recognised."
items.text: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in [[1966 => 1948]] by the United Nations [[Security Council => General Assembly]]. It is a [[binding treaty => non-binding declaration]]. In 1966 two covenants turned many of its rights into treaty obligations. Because Australia is a [[monist => dualist]] state, these treaties only become part of domestic law when parliament enacts them.

items.title: How a human rights treaty becomes Australian law
steps: States negotiate the text of the treaty
The treaty is adopted and opened for signature
Australia signs the treaty
The treaty is tabled in parliament and reviewed by a committee
Australia ratifies the treaty
Parliament passes legislation to give the treaty effect in domestic law
items.closing: Signing shows intent. Only legislation makes the rights enforceable in Australian courts.

items.q: Which international instrument recognises a right to adequate housing as part of an adequate standard of living?
o: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights

e.why: Article 11 of the Covenant covers an adequate standard of living, including housing. Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights says the same.

items.q: Which system of land registration is used for most land in NSW?

e.why: Torrens title, under the Real Property Act 1900 (NSW), relies on a central register guaranteed by the state.

items.q: A buyer purchases a house at auction in NSW. Which statement is correct?
o: The buyer has a five business day cooling-off period
The buyer has no cooling-off period
The buyer can withdraw at any time before settlement
The seller can accept a higher offer after the auction

e.why: The cooling-off period applies to private treaty sales only. An auction sale is binding when the hammer falls.

items.q: What does a buyer forfeit if they withdraw from a private treaty purchase during the cooling-off period in NSW?
o: 0.25 per cent of the purchase price
The cost of the seller's legal fees

e.why: The Conveyancing Act 1919 (NSW) lets the buyer withdraw but the seller keeps 0.25 per cent of the price.

items.q: What is the maximum rental bond a landlord can ask for in NSW?
o: Any amount the tenant agrees to

e.why: The Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) caps the bond at four weeks' rent. It must be lodged with NSW Fair Trading.

items.q: Which of the following is an obligation of a landlord under a residential tenancy agreement?
o: To pay the tenant's electricity bills
To keep the premises in a reasonable state of repair
To inspect the premises every week

e.why: The landlord must provide premises that are fit to live in and keep them in reasonable repair. Entry is limited and needs notice.

items.q: What changed for NSW tenants in May 2025?
o: Landlords could no longer end a tenancy without giving a reason set out in the law
Tenancy disputes moved to the District Court

e.why: Amendments to the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) ended "no grounds" evictions for both periodic and fixed-term leases.

items.q: Where would a tenant in NSW go to dispute a landlord's claim on their bond?
o: The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal
The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia

e.why: The Tribunal hears tenancy disputes cheaply and with little formality. Parties usually represent themselves.

items.q: Which is an example of alternative dispute resolution for neighbours arguing about a fence?
o: A trial in the District Court
Mediation at a Community Justice Centre
A complaint to the High Court

e.why: Community Justice Centres offer free mediation in NSW. The neighbours keep control of the outcome.

items.q: A landlord refuses to rent a flat to a woman because she has young children. Which NSW Act is most relevant?

e.why: The Act makes discrimination in accommodation unlawful on grounds that include sex, race, disability and responsibilities as a carer.

items.q: Which statement about homelessness in Australia is correct?
o: Most people counted as homeless are sleeping rough
People in severely crowded dwellings and temporary accommodation are counted as homeless

e.why: The Australian Bureau of Statistics counts several groups. People sleeping rough are a small share of the total.

items.q: What is the main purpose of social housing?
o: To give investors a tax deduction
To provide secure, affordable rental housing for people on low incomes who cannot afford the private market
To help first home buyers save a deposit

e.why: Social housing includes public, community and Aboriginal housing. Rent is usually set as a share of income.

items.q: Explain how the law protects a person buying a home in NSW.
pts: The seller must disclose documents in the contract for sale, such as the title search and the zoning certificate (1)
A cooling-off period applies to private treaty sales (1)
Torrens title guarantees the registered title (1)
Building and pest inspections are still the buyer's job: caveat emptor (1)

items.q: Explain the rights and obligations of tenants under the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW).
pts: Right to quiet enjoyment and to premises that are fit to live in (1)
Right to have urgent repairs done (1)
Limits on bonds, rent increases and landlord entry (1)
Obligation to pay rent on time and keep the premises reasonably clean (1)
Obligation not to cause damage or a nuisance (1)

items.q: Assess the effectiveness of government responses to housing affordability.
pts: Describes the problem with a statistic from a named source (1)
A response for buyers, such as stamp duty concessions or deposit guarantees (1)
A response for renters, such as Commonwealth Rent Assistance or tenancy reform (1)
A supply response, such as planning reform or housing targets (1)
A limit, such as demand-side measures pushing prices up (1)
A judgement (1)

items.lead: Mei rents a flat in Sydney on a 12-month lease. In month four the hot water system breaks. She emails the agent three times over two weeks and nothing happens. She pays a plumber $900 to fix it and asks the landlord to repay her. The landlord refuses and says she will be evicted for "causing trouble".

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Identify the landlord's obligation that has been breached.
pts: To keep the premises in reasonable repair (1)
A failed hot water service is an urgent repair (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain whether Mei can recover the $900.
pts: A tenant can arrange urgent repairs if the landlord cannot be contacted or does not act (1)
The landlord must repay reasonable costs up to the limit set by the regulations (1)
She should keep her notices and receipts as evidence (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain how the dispute could be resolved and whether the landlord's threat is lawful.
pts: She can apply to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal for an order (1)
The Tribunal can refuse to end a tenancy where the landlord's notice is retaliatory (1)
A landlord now needs a ground set out in the Act to end a tenancy (1)

items.lead: Sam and Alex find a house they love. The agent says another buyer is interested and urges them to sign today. They exchange contracts by private treaty on Monday and pay a deposit. On Wednesday a building inspector finds serious termite damage.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Outline what the cooling-off period allows Sam and Alex to do.
pts: Withdraw from the contract within five business days of exchange (1)
They forfeit 0.25 per cent of the price (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain how the outcome would differ if they had bought the house at auction.
pts: No cooling-off period applies at auction (1)
They would be bound to complete or lose their deposit (1)
Inspections must be done before bidding (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain what caveat emptor means for buyers.
pts: The buyer bears the risk of defects they could have found (1)
Buyers should get building, pest and strata reports before they commit (1)

items.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the law in protecting the rights of tenants.
pts: Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW): bonds, repairs, rent increases, entry
The 2025 reforms: the end of no-grounds evictions and rules on pets
The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal: cheap and fast, but tenants often do not use it
Boarders and lodgers: weaker protection
Discrimination and affordability as limits on rights in practice
Non-legal responses: the Tenants' Union, tenant advice services, the media
A judgement using criteria such as accessibility, enforceability and responsiveness

items.q: Assess the role of the law in responding to homelessness.
pts: The right to shelter in international law, and the lack of an enforceable right in Australia
Causes of homelessness: family violence, affordability, health
Legal responses: social housing, funding agreements between governments, tenancy protections
Non-legal responses: specialist homelessness services and charities
Limits: waiting lists, funding and supply
A judgement with statistics from a named source
plan: The scale of the problem and the right
Non-legal responses carry much of the load

Evidence: Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) and the complaint process
Analysis against enforceability: discrimination is hard to prove

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline how a tenancy begins and how disputes are resolved in NSW."
items.text: A tenancy in NSW is governed by the [[Real Property Act 1900 => Residential Tenancies Act 2010]] (NSW). The tenant pays a bond of up to [[eight => four]] weeks' rent, which must be lodged with [[the landlord's bank => NSW Fair Trading]]. Both sides sign a [[title deed => condition report]] that records the state of the property. If a dispute cannot be settled, either side can apply to the [[District Court => NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal]].

items.q: Which of the following is a reason for law reform?
o: Changing social values, new technology and the failure of existing law
The Constitution requires a new law every year

e.why: Law must keep up with society. When it falls behind, people lose confidence in it.

items.q: Laws on cyberbullying and image-based abuse were introduced mainly in response to which driver?
o: The cost of running the courts

e.why: Existing laws did not cover new kinds of harm made possible by smartphones and social media.

items.q: Which is a formal method of driving law reform?
o: A report by a law reform commission

e.why: Law reform commissions and royal commissions are set up by governments to inquire and recommend. Protests, campaigns and the media are informal methods.

items.q: What can a law reform commission do?
o: Research an area of law and recommend changes to the government

e.why: Commissions advise. Only parliament can enact their recommendations, and it does not have to.

items.q: How can courts change the law?
o: By interpreting statutes and creating precedents in the cases that come before them

e.why: Judges make law only when a case raises the issue. Parliament can override a decision by passing a statute.

items.q: Which is a limitation of law reform through parliament?
o: Reform can be slow and shaped by political interests
Parliament can only act when a case is brought
Acts of parliament apply to one person only

e.why: Governments may avoid controversial reforms or lack the numbers to pass them. Courts, not parliament, must wait for a case.

items.q: What did the High Court decide in Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992)?
o: That terra nullius applied to Australia
That native title exists at common law where traditional connection to the land has continued
That all freehold land must be returned
That the Constitution recognises Aboriginal sovereignty

e.why: The Court rejected terra nullius and recognised the native title of the Meriam people to the Murray Islands.

items.q: Which Act did the Commonwealth Parliament pass in response to the Mabo decision?

e.why: The Act set up a process for claiming native title and the National Native Title Tribunal.

items.q: How do land rights under the Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1983 (NSW) differ from native title?
o: Land rights are granted by statute and do not need proof of continuous traditional connection
Land rights come from the common law
Land rights apply only in the Torres Strait

e.why: Land councils can claim certain unused Crown land as compensation for dispossession. Native title recognises rights that have survived under traditional law and custom.

items.q: What does the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024 (Cth) require?
o: Parents must supervise all internet use
Age-restricted social media platforms must take reasonable steps to prevent people under 16 from having accounts
Children under 16 who use social media are fined

e.why: The duty is on the platforms, not on children or parents. The rules took effect on 10 December 2025.

items.q: Who enforces the social media minimum age law?

e.why: The eSafety Commissioner oversees compliance. Platforms that fail to take reasonable steps face large civil penalties.

items.q: Explain how the media can drive law reform.
pts: The media report on problems and individual cases (1)
Coverage shapes public opinion (1)
Public pressure reaches politicians, who respond to keep support (1)
An example of a law changed after a media campaign (1)

items.q: Explain how the Mabo decision led to changes in the law.
pts: The High Court rejected terra nullius in 1992 (1)
It recognised native title at common law (1)
The decision created uncertainty about land claims (1)
Parliament responded with the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) (1)
The case shows courts and parliament both making law (1)

items.q: Assess the benefits and limitations of the social media minimum age law as an example of law reform.
pts: Outlines the reform (1)
A benefit, such as protecting young people from online harm (1)
A second benefit, such as placing responsibility on platforms (1)
A limitation, such as difficulty verifying age or privacy concerns (1)
A second limitation, such as young people moving to less regulated services or losing connection (1)
A judgement (1)

items.trigger: Parents, researchers and the media raise concerns about the effect of social media on young people's mental health.

steps.v: Advocacy groups and media campaigns call for an age limit
Governments announce support for a minimum age
steps.why: Political will is needed before parliament acts.

steps.v: A bill is introduced into the Commonwealth Parliament
steps.why: Statute law is the fastest way to regulate a new problem.

steps.why: Both houses agreed to the bill.

steps.v: The eSafety Commissioner prepares to enforce the law
steps.why: An independent regulator is given the job.

steps.v: Platforms must take reasonable steps to keep under-16s from holding accounts

items.title: From the Murray Islands to the Native Title Act
items.trigger: In 1982 Eddie Koiki Mabo and other Meriam people begin a legal claim to their traditional lands.

steps.v: The case reaches the High Court
steps.why: Only the High Court could overturn the doctrine of terra nullius.

steps.v: The High Court rejects terra nullius in 1992
steps.why: The Court found the doctrine was wrong in fact and unjust.

steps.v: Native title is recognised at common law
steps.why: Traditional rights survived where connection continued and had not been extinguished.

steps.v: Governments, miners and farmers seek certainty
steps.why: No one knew which land could be claimed.

steps.v: Parliament passes the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth)
steps.why: Statute set up a process for claims.

items.title: How a law reform commission inquiry leads to a new law
steps: The Attorney-General gives the commission terms of reference
The commission researches the law and releases a discussion paper
The public and experts make submissions
The commission gives its final report with recommendations
The government decides which recommendations to accept
A bill is introduced and passed by parliament

items.q: Sort each example under the correct type of method for influencing law reform.

rows.t: A petition organised by an advocacy group

By deciding cases and interpreting statutes
Only when a case is brought
