Change is narrow and depends on someone bringing a case

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline the significance of the Mabo decision."
items.text: In [[1982 => 1992]] the [[Supreme Court of Queensland => High Court of Australia]] decided Mabo v Queensland (No 2). The Court [[confirmed => rejected]] the doctrine of terra nullius and recognised [[land rights => native title]] at common law. The next year parliament passed the [[Aboriginal Land Rights Act => Native Title Act]] 1993 (Cth).

items.q: Who brings a criminal case to court?
o: The state, through the police or the Director of Public Prosecutions

e.why: A crime is treated as a wrong against the whole community, so the state prosecutes.

items.q: What must the prosecution prove for most criminal offences?

e.why: The physical act and the guilty mind must both be proved. Strict liability offences are the exception.

items.lead: A driver is fined for travelling 15 km/h over the speed limit. She says she did not notice the sign.
items.q: Why is she still liable?
o: Speeding is a strict liability offence, so intention need not be proved
She has the burden of proving her innocence beyond reasonable doubt

e.why: For strict liability offences the prosecution proves the act only.

items.q: What is the standard of proof in a civil case?

e.why: The plaintiff must show their version is more likely than not.

items.q: Which case established the modern law of negligence and the "neighbour principle"?

e.why: In 1932 the House of Lords held that a manufacturer owed a duty of care to the person who consumed its product.

items.q: What must a plaintiff prove to succeed in a negligence claim?
o: A duty of care, a breach of that duty, and damage caused by the breach

e.why: These are the elements of negligence. Offer, acceptance and consideration are elements of a contract.

items.q: Which of the following is needed for a valid contract?
o: A written document signed in front of a witness
Offer, acceptance, consideration and an intention to create legal relations

e.why: Many contracts are verbal. The elements, not the form, make an agreement binding.

items.q: What is the most common remedy in a civil case?
o: A fine paid to the state

e.why: Civil remedies aim to compensate the person who was wronged. Fines and imprisonment are criminal sanctions.

items.q: A person wants an independent body to take a fresh look at a Commonwealth visa decision and, if it is wrong, change it. Which process is this?

e.why: Merits review, by a body such as the Administrative Review Tribunal, reconsiders the facts, law and policy. Judicial review only asks whether the decision was lawful.

items.q: Which body investigates complaints about the conduct of NSW government agencies?

e.why: The Ombudsman is independent, free to use and can recommend changes, but cannot usually force an agency to act.

items.q: Which is an advantage of using a tribunal rather than a court?
o: Tribunals are usually cheaper, quicker and less formal
Tribunal decisions can never be appealed

e.why: Tribunals such as the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal are designed to be accessible to people without lawyers.

items.q: Distinguish between criminal law and civil law.
pts: Purpose: criminal law punishes and protects the community; civil law compensates (1)
Parties: the state against an accused; a plaintiff against a defendant (1)
Standard of proof: beyond reasonable doubt; balance of probabilities (1)
Outcome: guilty and a sanction; liable and a remedy (1)

items.q: Explain TWO ways a person can challenge a decision made by a government agency.
pts: Names and explains one way, such as internal review, merits review by a tribunal, a complaint to the Ombudsman or judicial review by a court (2)
Names and explains a second way (2)

items.q: Assess the effectiveness of alternative dispute resolution in resolving civil disputes.
pts: Describes a method, such as mediation (1)
Strengths: lower cost, speed and privacy (1)
The parties keep control and relationships are preserved (1)
Limits: an imbalance of power, no binding precedent, and the need for cooperation (1)
A judgement (1)

items.lead: Ben buys a takeaway salad from a cafe. Halfway through eating it he finds a piece of broken glass and cuts his mouth. He needs stitches and misses three days of work. The cafe owner says a jar broke in the kitchen that morning and the staff "thought they had cleaned it all up".

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Explain whether the cafe owed Ben a duty of care and whether it was breached.
pts: A business that sells food owes a duty of care to its customers (1)
Harm from glass in food is reasonably foreseeable (1)
Serving food after a jar broke nearby, without proper checks, is a failure to take reasonable care (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Identify the remedy Ben would seek and what it would cover.
pts: Damages (1)
Medical costs, lost wages, and pain and suffering (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain why Ben's case is a civil matter and not a criminal one.
pts: It is a dispute between private parties about compensation (1)
Ben, as plaintiff, must prove his case on the balance of probabilities (1)

items.lead: Lina's application for a disability support payment is refused by a Commonwealth agency. The letter gives no clear reasons. She believes the officer ignored her doctor's report.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Outline the first steps Lina should take.
pts: Ask the agency for reasons and for an internal review (1)
Keep to the time limits for review (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain how a tribunal could help if the internal review fails.
pts: The Administrative Review Tribunal can conduct a merits review (1)
It looks at the evidence afresh, including the doctor's report (1)
It can affirm, vary or set aside the decision (1)

items.title: Steps in a civil dispute
steps: The dispute arises
The parties try to negotiate
A letter of demand is sent
The parties attend mediation
The plaintiff files a statement of claim
The court hears the case
The court gives judgment and orders a remedy
items.closing: Most civil disputes settle before a hearing.

items.q: Sort each term under the type of case it belongs to.
Complete the table to compare two ways of reviewing a government decision.

cells.t: Was this the correct or preferable decision?
The decision can be set aside and sent back to be made again

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline the difference between criminal and civil cases."
items.text: In a criminal case the [[plaintiff => prosecution]] must prove the offence [[on the balance of probabilities => beyond reasonable doubt]]. If the accused is found guilty, the court imposes a [[remedy => sanction]]. In a civil case the person who sues is called the [[accused => plaintiff]], and a successful claim usually ends in an award of damages.

items.q: Why does the law give young people special protection?
o: Young people have more money than adults
Young people are still developing and are more vulnerable to harm and exploitation
Young people cannot break the law

e.why: The law recognises limited maturity and experience, while giving more independence as capacity grows.

items.q: What is the minimum age of criminal responsibility in NSW?

e.why: A child under 10 cannot be charged. From 10 to under 14, doli incapax applies.

items.q: What does a high rate of recidivism among young people who have been in detention suggest?
o: Detention is working well as a deterrent
Detention often fails to address the causes of offending
Young people commit more serious crimes than adults
The age of criminal responsibility is too high

e.why: If many young people reoffend after detention, rehabilitation has not been achieved. This supports diversion.

items.q: Which international treaty sets out the rights of people under 18?
o: Convention on the Rights of the Child
International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights

e.why: Australia ratified the Convention in 1990. It says the best interests of the child must be a primary consideration.

items.q: Which NSW court hears most criminal matters involving people under 18?

e.why: The Children's Court is a closed, specialist court. Very serious offences can be sent to a higher court.

items.q: Which Act sets up warnings, cautions and youth justice conferences in NSW?

e.why: The Act diverts young people who admit less serious offences away from court.

items.q: Which body advocates for the rights of children and young people across Australia?

e.why: The Commissioner sits within the Australian Human Rights Commission. NSW also has an Advocate for Children and Young People.

items.q: Which is a barrier to justice for many young people?
o: They are not allowed to have a lawyer
They often do not know their rights or how to get legal help
Courts are open only on weekends

e.why: Lack of knowledge, cost, distance and distrust of authority all limit access. Legal Aid NSW runs a Youth Hotline to help.

items.q: What is the difference between an asylum seeker and a refugee?
o: An asylum seeker has been found to be owed protection; a refugee has not
An asylum seeker's claim for protection has not yet been decided; a refugee meets the legal definition
A refugee always arrives by boat

e.why: Every refugee was first an asylum seeker. How a person arrives does not decide whether they are a refugee.

items.q: Which treaty defines who is a refugee and sets out the duty of non-refoulement?
o: Convention on the Rights of the Child
Convention relating to the Status of Refugees (1951)

e.why: The Convention and its 1967 Protocol bind Australia in international law.

items.q: Which Act governs visas, detention and the removal of non-citizens in Australia?

e.why: The Act requires the detention of unlawful non-citizens and sets the tests for protection visas.

items.q: What did the High Court decide in NZYQ v Minister for Immigration (2023)?
o: That indefinite immigration detention is unlawful where there is no real prospect of removing the person in the reasonably foreseeable future
That all asylum seekers must be given permanent visas
That the Refugee Convention is part of the Constitution

e.why: The decision overturned Al-Kateb v Godwin (2004) and led to the release of people held in long-term detention.

items.q: Which body can review many decisions to refuse a protection visa?
o: The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal

e.why: The Tribunal replaced the Administrative Appeals Tribunal in October 2024 and conducts merits review of Commonwealth decisions.

items.q: Explain what is meant by the "evolving capacity" of young people, using TWO examples of age limits in the law.
pts: Defines evolving capacity (1)
The law gives rights and responsibilities in stages (1)
Two accurate examples, such as criminal responsibility at 10, a learner licence at 16 or voting at 18 (2)

items.q: Explain how the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) aims to achieve justice for young people.
pts: It provides warnings, cautions and youth justice conferences (1)
Court is kept for more serious matters (1)
Young people avoid a criminal record for minor offending (1)
Conferences let victims take part and repair harm (1)
A limit, such as uneven use across groups (1)

items.q: Assess the responsiveness of the legal system to asylum seekers and refugees.
pts: An indicator of success, such as merits review or access to the courts (1)
A case or law that shows it, such as NZYQ (2023) (1)
A barrier, such as mandatory detention or offshore processing (1)
A second barrier, such as delay, language or limited legal aid (1)
The role of advocates, such as the Australian Human Rights Commission or non-government organisations (1)
A judgement (1)

items.lead: Kai, aged 15, is stopped by police at a train station after a security guard says he saw Kai take a pair of headphones from a shop. Kai admits he took them. It is his first contact with police. The officer wants to take a formal statement from him straight away, on the platform.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Outline TWO rights Kai has when police question him.
pts: The right to silence, apart from giving his name and address (1)
The right to have a responsible adult present and to get legal advice, for example from the Legal Aid Youth Hotline (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain the most likely outcome for Kai and why.
pts: A caution, or possibly a warning, under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) (1)
The offence is minor, he admits it and it is his first (1)
Diversion aims to keep young people out of court (1)

items.lead: Samira fled her country after she was threatened because of her work as a journalist. She arrived in Australia on a student visa and has now applied for a protection visa. A departmental officer refuses her application, saying she could safely live in another part of her country.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Explain whether Samira is an asylum seeker or a refugee at this point.
pts: She is an asylum seeker because her claim has not been finally decided (1)
She would be a refugee if she is found to have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention reason, such as political opinion (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Outline what Samira can do about the refusal.
pts: Apply for merits review by the Administrative Review Tribunal (1)
Seek help from a refugee legal service or advocacy group (1)
Judicial review by a court is possible if there was a legal error (1)

rows.cat: Indicator of success in achieving justice

People do not know their rights
Legal help is not funded for many cases
Detention far from family and lawyers

items.q: Complete the table to compare how two groups experience the law.

cells.t: Convention on the Rights of the Child
Convention relating to the Status of Refugees
Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) and Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW)
The department, the Administrative Review Tribunal and the federal courts
Australian Human Rights Commission or a refugee legal service

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline how the law treats a 12-year-old accused of an offence in NSW."
items.text: In NSW a child under [[12 => 10]] cannot be charged with an offence. A 12-year-old is covered by doli incapax, which means the [[defence => prosecution]] must prove the child knew the act was seriously wrong. The matter would be heard in the [[Local Court => Children's Court]], which is [[open => closed]] to the public.

items.q: Explain how laws are made in Australia. In your answer, refer to both parliament and the courts.
pts: Statute law: the stages of a bill and royal assent
Common law: precedent, ratio decidendi and the court hierarchy
The relationship between the two: statute overrides common law; courts interpret statutes
The Constitution sets the limits of law-making power
At least one named Act and one named case

items.q: Compare how criminal law and civil law resolve disputes.
pts: Purpose, parties, burden and standard of proof
Process: prosecution and trial against claim, negotiation and hearing
Outcomes: sanctions against remedies
A named example or case for each
Similarities as well as differences
plan: Conclusion: two systems for two kinds of wrong

items.q: Assess the outcomes of law reform in relation to native title.
pts: Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992) and the rejection of terra nullius
Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) and later amendments
Benefits: recognition, successful claims, agreements over land use
Limitations: the burden of proving continuous connection, extinguishment, delay and cost
A judgement

items.q: To what extent does the legal system achieve justice for young people?
pts: Protection in domestic and international law
Police powers and safeguards for young people
The Children's Court and diversion under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW)
Barriers: knowledge, access to legal help, over-representation of some groups, detention
A judgement on extent, with evidence

items.q: Assess the responsiveness of the legal system to asylum seekers and refugees.
pts: International obligations: the Refugee Convention and non-refoulement
Migration Act 1958 (Cth): detention and visas
Review by the Administrative Review Tribunal and the courts, including NZYQ (2023)
Advocates: the Australian Human Rights Commission and non-government organisations
Barriers: delay, detention, limited legal help
A judgement

items.q: Explain why the rule of law is important in Australia.
pts: A clear statement of what the rule of law means
Evidence: an example such as courts reviewing government decisions
Explanation of how it limits power
Counterpoint: unequal access to legal help weakens equality before the law
A link back to the question

items.q: Assess the effectiveness of tribunals in resolving disputes between individuals and the state.
pts: A judgement
Evidence: a named tribunal and what it can do
Analysis against accessibility or resource efficiency
Counterpoint: delay, or limits on what can be reviewed
A link back to the question

items.q: Assess the effectiveness of the social media minimum age law as a response to changing technology.
pts: A judgement
Evidence: Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024 (Cth) and who must comply
Analysis against enforceability or responsiveness
Counterpoint: age checks can be avoided, and there are privacy concerns
A link back to the question

items.q: Assess the effectiveness of diversion in achieving justice for young people.
pts: A judgement
Evidence: Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) and a finding from a named source
Analysis against the capacity to meet society's needs
Counterpoint: diversion is not used equally for all groups
A link back to the question

items.q: What is the main difference between a law and a rule?
o: Laws are written down; rules are not
Laws apply to everyone in society and are enforced by the state
Rules carry heavier penalties than laws
Laws are made by schools and clubs

e.why: Rules apply to members of a group, such as a school. Laws bind the whole community and are enforced by police and courts.

items.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of an effective law?
o: It is kept secret until it is enforced
It is known, clear and able to be enforced
It applies only to some people

e.why: People can only obey laws they can find out about and understand, and a law that cannot be enforced will be ignored.

items.q: A person sues a builder for failing to finish a house. Which area of law is this?

e.why: A dispute between individuals over a contract is private law. The state is not a party.

items.q: How is Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Customary Lore traditionally passed on?
o: Orally, through stories, song, dance and ceremony

e.why: Customary Lore is an oral tradition. Elders hold the knowledge and pass it on to the next generation.

items.q: Which statement about Customary Lore is most accurate?
o: It is the same for all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
It differs between nations and language groups but shares common features, such as connection to Country
It deals only with criminal matters
It was created by the British in 1788

e.why: There are many nations, each with its own Lore. Shared features include kinship, Country and the role of Elders.

items.q: Which part of a judgment creates a binding precedent?

e.why: The ratio decidendi is the legal reasoning needed for the decision. Lower courts in the same hierarchy must follow it.

items.q: A District Court judge in NSW is deciding a case. Which decision is binding on that judge?
o: A decision of the Local Court
A decision of the Supreme Court of Victoria
A decision of the High Court of Australia
A decision of a court in England

e.why: Decisions of higher courts in the same hierarchy bind lower courts. Decisions from other hierarchies are persuasive only.

items.q: What is the final step before a bill becomes an Act?

e.why: After both houses pass the bill, the Governor-General (or a state Governor) gives royal assent.

items.q: Which is the highest court in Australia?

e.why: The High Court is the final court of appeal and decides cases about the Constitution.

items.q: What is the role of the Coroner's Court?
o: To sentence people convicted of murder
To inquire into the cause and manner of unexplained deaths, and into fires and explosions
To hear appeals from the Local Court

e.why: A coroner holds an inquest to make findings and recommendations. A coroner does not decide guilt.

items.q: What happens under s 109 of the Constitution when a valid Commonwealth law and a state law are inconsistent?
o: The Commonwealth law prevails and the state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency
The High Court holds a referendum

e.why: Section 109 settles clashes in areas of concurrent power in favour of the Commonwealth.

items.q: What is needed for a referendum to change the Constitution to succeed?
o: A majority in the House of Representatives only
A majority of voters nationally and a majority of voters in a majority of states
The agreement of all six state premiers
A unanimous decision of the High Court

e.why: Section 128 requires this double majority. Only 8 of 45 proposals have passed.

items.q: Which arm of government interprets and applies the law?

e.why: The legislature makes law, the executive carries it out and the judiciary (the courts) interprets it.

items.q: What is a treaty?
o: A law passed by the United Nations that binds every country
A written agreement between states that binds the states that ratify it
A decision of the International Court of Justice
A custom followed within one country

e.why: Treaties bind only the states that agree to them. In Australia a treaty also needs legislation before it applies in domestic law.

items.q: Which of the following is a source of rights in Australia?
o: The Constitution, statute law, common law and international law

e.why: Australia has no national bill of rights. Rights come from several sources, each with limits.

items.q: Explain how the doctrine of precedent promotes fairness and consistency.
pts: Courts follow earlier decisions of higher courts in the same hierarchy (1)
Like cases are decided alike (1)
People and lawyers can predict how the law will apply (1)
Judges can still distinguish a case on its facts, which allows the law to develop (1)

items.q: Explain why the separation of powers is important.
pts: Names the three arms and what each does (1)
No single body makes, carries out and judges the law (1)
Independent courts can check the other arms (1)
This protects individuals from the abuse of power (1)

items.q: Describe the role of Elders in maintaining Customary Lore.
pts: Elders hold knowledge of Lore and pass it on (1)
They teach through story, ceremony and example (1)
They help resolve disputes through discussion and mediation (1)
They are involved in programs such as circle sentencing (1)

items.q: Explain how state sovereignty affects the enforcement of international law.
pts: Defines state sovereignty (1)
States choose whether to sign and ratify treaties (1)
There is no world police force; enforcement relies on cooperation and pressure (1)
An example of a state not complying (1)
Sovereignty also lets states pass laws to give effect to their obligations (1)

items.lead: The NSW Parliament passes a law that says shops may refuse to accept cash. A year later the Commonwealth Parliament passes a valid law, under its currency power, that says all shops must accept cash for purchases under $500. A shop owner in Sydney does not know which law to follow.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Identify the section of the Constitution that resolves this conflict.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain which law the shop owner must follow and why.
pts: The Commonwealth law (1)
Where a valid Commonwealth law and a state law are inconsistent, the Commonwealth law prevails (1)
The state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency (1)

items.title: How a bill becomes an Act of the Commonwealth Parliament
steps: The bill is drafted
First reading: the bill is introduced
Second reading: the minister explains the bill and it is debated
Consideration in detail: the bill is examined clause by clause
Third reading: the house votes on the bill
The bill goes through the same stages in the other house
The Governor-General gives royal assent
items.closing: A bill must pass both houses in the same form before royal assent.

steps: Local Court
District Court
Supreme Court
Court of Criminal Appeal
High Court of Australia

cells.t: Case by case, as disputes arise
By passing, amending or repealing an Act

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline how the Australian Constitution can be changed."
items.text: The Constitution came into effect on 1 January [[1900 => 1901]]. It can be changed only by a referendum under section [[109 => 128]]. A proposal must first be passed by [[the High Court => Parliament]]. It then needs a majority of voters across Australia and a majority of voters in at least [[three => four]] of the six states. This is called a [[simple => double]] majority.

items.q: Which is an example of the changing nature of crime?
o: The growth of online fraud, scams and identity theft
The abolition of all summary offences
The removal of juries from every trial

e.why: Technology has created new offences and new ways to commit old ones, and the law has had to respond.

items.q: How does police discretion support the rule of law when it is used properly?
o: It lets police respond in proportion to the offence, within limits set by law and guidelines
It replaces the role of the courts
It applies only to indictable offences

e.why: Warnings, cautions and fines save court time for serious matters. The risk is inconsistent or biased use.

items.q: Why can a long period on remand be seen as conflicting with the presumption of innocence?
o: Remand is a sentence imposed after conviction
A person on remand is held in custody although they have not been found guilty
Remand applies only to people who plead guilty
People on remand cannot have a lawyer

e.why: Time on remand can cost a person their job or housing, and some are later acquitted or given a non-custodial sentence.

items.q: Which is an example of a pre-trial process?
o: An appeal to the High Court

e.why: Pre-trial steps decide whether and how a matter goes to trial, and encourage early guilty pleas.

items.q: Which is an argument for a judge-alone trial rather than a jury trial?
o: A judge gives written reasons, and the trial avoids jurors being swayed by pre-trial publicity
A judge represents a cross-section of the community
The accused cannot appeal a jury verdict

e.why: Reasons make the decision open to review. The main argument for juries is community participation.

items.q: Which organisation provides legal services designed for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in NSW?

e.why: The Service gives culturally appropriate advice and representation, including through the custody notification service.

items.q: Which is a diversionary program available to some adult offenders in NSW?

e.why: The Drug Court supervises treatment for drug-dependent offenders as an alternative to prison.

items.q: Which sentencing options are designed to be culturally appropriate for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander offenders?
o: Circle sentencing and the Youth Koori Court
Mandatory sentencing and standard non-parole periods

e.why: Elders and respected community members take part, which aims to make the process meaningful and to reduce reoffending.

items.q: Who decides how a prisoner in NSW is classified and where they are placed?

e.why: Classification reflects risk and affects access to programs and work, and so to rehabilitation.

items.q: What is the main criticism of continuing detention orders for high-risk offenders?
o: They are made by police without any court hearing
They keep a person in custody after their sentence has ended, on the basis of what they might do

e.why: The orders protect the community but sit uneasily with the principle that a person is punished only for what they have done.

items.q: Why do nation-states need international relations?
o: Because problems such as conflict, trade, climate and migration cross borders and cannot be solved by one state alone
Because the United Nations makes laws for every state
Because state sovereignty no longer exists
Because every state has the same legal system

e.why: Cooperation through treaties and organisations lets states manage shared problems while keeping their sovereignty.

items.q: Which is an example of a regional intergovernmental organisation?
o: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)
The International Committee of the Red Cross

e.why: Its members are states. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch are non-government organisations.

items.q: Which statement about the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples is correct?
o: It is a binding treaty enforced by the International Criminal Court
It is a non-binding declaration that sets standards, including the right to self-determination
It replaced the Universal Declaration of Human Rights

e.why: The General Assembly adopted it in 2007. Australia voted against it then and endorsed it in 2009.

items.q: How does the Universal Periodic Review monitor human rights?
o: Judges try the leaders of each state
The human rights record of every United Nations member state is reviewed by other states through the Human Rights Council
The Security Council inspects each state every year

e.why: The review produces recommendations. States are not forced to accept them.

items.q: What does the Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Act 2011 (Cth) require?
o: Courts must strike down laws that breach human rights
Each new bill must come with a statement of compatibility with human rights, and a parliamentary committee examines bills
A referendum on a bill of rights

e.why: The Act builds rights into law-making, but parliament can still pass a law that is not compatible.

items.q: Which is a limit on the role of the media in promoting human rights?
o: The media cannot report on other countries
Coverage can be selective, short-lived or shaped by commercial and political interests
The media is controlled by the United Nations
Journalists are not allowed to interview victims

e.why: Media attention can force action, but issues that are not covered may be ignored.

items.q: How does Australian law respond to forced marriage?
o: It is a criminal offence under Commonwealth law
It is lawful with parental consent
It is dealt with only by the Children's Court
It is not recognised as a legal issue

e.why: Forced marriage offences were added to the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) in 2013. Under-reporting makes cases hard to identify.

items.q: What is the aim of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Child Placement Principle?
o: To place every child in residential care
To keep children who cannot live at home connected to family, community, culture and Country
To move child protection cases to the High Court

e.why: The Principle responds to the harm done by past removal policies and is part of NSW child protection law.

items.q: What makes a financial agreement between partners binding under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth)?
o: It is in writing, signed, and each person has had independent legal advice
It is approved by the Children's Court
It is made after a divorce only

e.why: Without independent advice for each person, a court can set the agreement aside.

items.q: How does native title differ from Torrens title?
o: Native title is a registered freehold interest that can be sold
Native title recognises rights under traditional laws and customs and cannot be sold like freehold
Torrens title applies only to Crown land

e.why: Native title is a communal set of rights that depends on continuing connection. Torrens title is ownership recorded on the state register.

items.q: Why is culturally appropriate housing important for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples?
o: Housing designed and managed with communities supports kinship obligations, connection to Country and better health
It is required by the Constitution
It replaces the need for land rights

e.why: Standard housing and rules can clash with family obligations, and overcrowding harms health and education.

items.q: Which is a barrier to justice in property disputes?
o: The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal charges no fees at all
Complex rules, legal costs and language barriers discourage people from enforcing their rights
Tenants are banned from applying to the Tribunal

e.why: Rights that people cannot use in practice give little protection. Advice services and interpreters reduce the barrier.

items.q: Explain the impact of remand on the accused and on society.
pts: Defines remand (1)
Impact on the accused: loss of liberty, work, housing or family contact before any finding of guilt (1)
It is harder to prepare a defence from custody (1)
Impact on society: protection from risk, but a high cost and crowded prisons (1)
A link to the presumption of innocence (1)

items.q: Outline TWO reasons for and TWO reasons against the use of juries in criminal trials.
pts: For: community participation; the decision is shared among twelve people (2)
Against: no reasons are given; jurors may be influenced by the media or struggle with complex evidence (2)

items.q: Explain the purpose of parole and the conditions that may apply.
pts: Supervised release for the last part of a sentence (1)
It supports reintegration and reduces reoffending (1)
Conditions such as reporting, where to live and attending programs (1)
Parole can be revoked if conditions are breached (1)

items.q: Explain the impact of state sovereignty on the changing global community.
pts: Defines state sovereignty (1)
States remain the main actors and must consent to be bound (1)
Global problems and organisations put pressure on sovereignty (1)
An example, such as a state refusing to follow a decision of an international body (1)

items.q: Discuss the debate over the need for a human rights framework in Australia.
pts: Current protection is spread across the Constitution, statute and common law (1)
For: clearer rights, protection of minorities, education (1 to 2)
Against: parliamentary sovereignty, power shifted to judges, cost (1 to 2)
Refers to an existing model, such as the Victorian Charter or the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) (1)
Presents both sides (1)

items.q: Explain the challenges in identifying and responding to forced marriage in Australia.
pts: Defines forced marriage and notes it is a crime (1)
Victims are often young and under family pressure, so they may not report (1)
Marriages may take place overseas (1)
Responses include support services, protection orders and education (1)

items.q: Explain the impact of homelessness on the enjoyment of human rights.
pts: Names the right to adequate housing (1)
Health: harder to stay well or get treatment (1)
Education and work: hard to attend without a stable address (1)
Safety and privacy are at risk (1)
Rights are connected: losing one affects the others (1)

items.lead: Dev, aged 28, is charged with a serious assault. He has no criminal record, a full-time job and lives with his parents. The alleged victim is a neighbour. The case has been in the news for a week, with headlines calling Dev a "thug". His trial in the District Court is nine months away.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Explain what a court would consider in deciding whether to grant Dev bail.
pts: Whether there is an unacceptable risk, such as endangering the victim or interfering with witnesses (1)
His community ties, job and lack of record reduce the risk of failing to appear (1)
Conditions, such as no contact with the neighbour, could manage the risk (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain why Dev might apply for a judge-alone trial.
pts: Pre-trial publicity may prejudice jurors (1)
A judge gives reasons, which can be tested on appeal (1)
The court decides whether a judge-alone trial is in the interests of justice (1)

items.lead: Thanh arrived in Australia two years ago and speaks limited English. He rents a unit with his family. Mould has spread through the bedroom and his daughter's asthma is worse. The agent has ignored his messages for a month. Thanh is afraid that if he complains, the family will lose their home.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Identify the landlord's obligation and the body that can enforce it.
pts: To provide and maintain premises that are fit to live in and in reasonable repair (1)
The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain the barriers Thanh faces in accessing justice and how they could be reduced.
pts: Language: forms and hearings are in English (1)
Fear of losing the tenancy, and not knowing the law (1)
Interpreters are available at the Tribunal, and tenant advice services give free help (1)
The law limits retaliatory evictions and now requires a reason to end a tenancy (1)

items.q: To what extent do sentencing and post-sentencing measures balance the rights of victims, offenders and society?
pts: The purposes of sentencing and how they compete
Judicial discretion, guidelines, and aggravating and mitigating factors
Victim impact statements
Custodial and non-custodial penalties, with evidence on reoffending
Diversionary and culturally appropriate options
Parole, and detention and supervision orders for high-risk offenders
A sustained judgement
plan: Victims: a voice but not a veto
Society: protection after the sentence ends

items.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of legal and non-legal measures in protecting ONE human right.
pts: Names the right and where it is recognised
International protection: instruments, monitoring and courts, and their limits
Australian protection: the Constitution, statute, common law, the Australian Human Rights Commission, courts and tribunals
Promotion by non-government organisations and the media
A judgement using criteria such as enforceability and the protection of individual rights
plan: Domestic protection without a national framework

pts: A judgement

Analysis against resource efficiency or the capacity to meet society's needs
Counterpoint: limited places and strict eligibility

pts: A judgement
Evidence: a named measure and a statistic from a named source
Analysis against the capacity to meet society's needs

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline how high-risk offenders can be managed after their sentence ends in NSW."
items.text: Under the Crimes (High Risk Offenders) Act 2006 (NSW), the [[Local Court => Supreme Court]] can make orders about serious sex or violence offenders who still pose an unacceptable risk. An [[intensive correction => extended supervision]] order lets the person live in the community under strict conditions. A continuing [[parole => detention]] order keeps the person in custody. These orders are made [[before the trial => near the end of the sentence]].
